BASIC DEFINITIONS
Topography is the study of the shape, height, and surface features of
land.
A mountain is a very high landform with steep sides and a peak (top).
A plateau is a high flat land area raised above the surrounding land.
A gorge is a deep, narrow valley with steep sides, usually formed by a
river.
A cuesta is a long ridge with a gentle slope on one side and a steep slope
on the other side.
A valley is a low area of land between hills or mountains, often with a
river flowing through it.
A glacier is a large mass of moving ice formed from snow in very cold
areas.
A hamun is a shallow seasonal lake found in dry areas, which fills with
water during rains and dries up later.

BASIC DEFINITIONS
Irrigation: The artificial supply of water to crops to help them grow, especially in
dry areas.
Underground Water: Water stored beneath the Earth’s surface in soil and rock
layers.
Water Table: The upper level of groundwater below the Earth’s surface.
River – A natural stream of flowing water that moves towards a sea, lake, or
another river.
Canal: A man-made waterway used to carry water for irrigation, transport, or
other purposes.
Reservoir: A large artificial lake where water is stored behind a dam.
Groundwater – Water stored beneath the Earth's surface in soil and rocks.
Aquifer: An underground layer of rock or soil that stores and supplies
groundwater.
Waterlogging: A condition where excess water collects in the soil, reducing crop
growth.
Salinity: The presence of excessive salts in the soil, making farming difficult.
Water Table: The upper level of groundwater beneath the Earth's surface.
Basin: An area of land drained by a river and its tributaries. All the water in a
basin flows towards the same main river.

These create scenic beauty which promotes tourism in country.
Rivers help to generate Hydro Electric Power (HEP).
These enhance the fertility of soil by spreading fresh alluvium.
Fishing is practiced in rivers thus provides jobs for local people.
These provide water for irrigation through canals.
These provide water for domestic and industrial uses.

transport minerals. For example, coal mining in Thar provides jobs for local people. This
increases their income and improves their standard of living.
Mining provides raw materials for industries. For example, limestone is used in cement
factories, while coal can be used as a source of energy. This helps industries grow and
increases industrial production.
Mineral exports can earn foreign exchange. Minerals such as copper and gold can be sold
to other countries. For example, Saindak and Reko Diq have large copper and gold
deposits. Export earnings can help Pakistan pay for imports.
Mining increases government revenue because mining companies pay taxes, royalties
and other charges. The government can use this money to improve facilities such as
roads, schools and hospitals.
Mining can develop remote areas. New mines require roads, electricity, water supplies
and communication facilities. For example, mining development in Balochistan and Thar
can improve infrastructure in areas that were previously less developed.

PROBLEMS OF MINING INDUSTRIES
Lack of finance: Pakistan does not have enough money to invest in the exploration
of minerals. A number of institutions have been working for the development of
mineral sector but that is unsuccessful.
Lack of technical experts: Mining requires high tech experts with in-depth
theoretical and practical knowledge of geology, computerized mining operations,
specialized mining machinery. Pakistan is lagging in this.
Inaccessible mineral deposits: Due to poor infrastructure (Roads and railway) or bad
land elevated topography, there is so much difficulty to reach out those areas for
mining.
Security issues: After increasing terrorist activities in Pakistan specially in
Balochistan (also due to tribal opposition) many mining companies are reluctant to
carry out their mining operations in Pakistan.
Mismanagement: Mineral offices are also victims of corruption and low standards of
work. This has resulted in low standards of work. This has resulted in low
productivity in the mining sector.

WHY NO FISHING IN COASTAL AREAS FROM MAY
TO SEPTEMBER?
South-west monsoon winds blow from May to September -- these winds make the sea
rough and dangerous -- making it difficult for fishing boats to operate safely.
Heavy rainfall and poor visibility during the monsoon can also make fishing more
dangerous.
At the same time, many fish species breed during the monsoon season -- fishing is
reduced to allow fish to reproduce and maintain fish stocks.
IMPORTANCE OF MANGROVE IN FISHING
Mangrove forest provides breeding place for shrimp and fish.
Falling leaves and fruit of mangrove provide nutrients (food) to fish.
The roots of mangrove protect small fish from predators (big fish).
Roots of mangrove also trap nutrients brought by river.
IMPORTANCE OF FISHING
Provides employment to thousands of people in coastal areas
Source of food and protein for the population
Helps in earning foreign exchange through fish exports
Helps in the development of fishing industries (like fish processing and packaging)
CHALLENGES FACED BY FISHING INDUSTRY
Overfishing has decreased quantity of fish catch in sea; many types of fish have became
extinct.
Water pollution and oil spills have affected fish production.
Loss of breeding areas and shelter due to deforestation of mangrove forest.
Fishing is closed in breeding season.
Fishing on large scale by foreign boats in marine water of Pakistan.
There is a ban on canned fish of Pakistan by Western countries.
HOW FISHING METHODS CAN BE IMPROVED?
Boats with engine can go further in sea and can stay for longer time in sea.
Cold storage in boats can keep fish fresh.
Winches in boats can pull long net from sea along with fish.
Sonar can be used to locate fish.
Bigger and stronger nets can catch large quantity of fish.
Radio can be used for communication (contact) in case of emergency.
Fishermen can use modern fishing methods by education and training.
Weather forecast can warn about bad weather.

CHALLENGES FACED BY FISHING INDUSTRY
Overfishing has decreased quantity of fish catch in sea; many types of fish have became
extinct.
Water pollution and oil spills have affected fish production.
Loss of breeding areas and shelter due to deforestation of mangrove forest.
Fishing is closed in breeding season.
Fishing on large scale by foreign boats in marine water of Pakistan.
There is a ban on canned fish of Pakistan by Western countries.
STEPS TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT TO
DEVELOP FISHING IN PAKISTAN
A.D.B.P (Agricultural development bank of Pakistan) provides loans to fisher men.
Provincial fisheries department provide technical help.
Government has set up hatcheries to provide small fish to fish farms.
Fisheries training centers are set up to provide training to fisher men.
Cold storages are setup for fish storage.
Processing centers are set up for cleaning, preserving and packing fish.
HOW TO MAKE FISHING SUSTAINABLE?
Possibilities :
Set fishing quotas to limit the number of fish caught each year. Example: Pakistan can set
a limit on the amount of fish fishermen can catch.
Ban fishing during the breeding season so fish can reproduce. Example: Fishing can be
stopped during breeding months along the Sindh coast.
Use larger-holed nets so small fish can escape and grow. Example: Young fish can pass
through the net.
Reduce pollution in seas and rivers to protect fish habitats. Example: Industrial waste
should not be dumped into the Arabian Sea.
Encourage fish farming so less pressure is placed on Marine fish.
Challenges:
Lack of money makes it difficult to monitor large coastal areas. Example: Pakistan has a
long coastline that is difficult to monitor.
Fishermen may oppose fishing restrictions because fishing is their source of income.
Example: A seasonal ban may temporarily reduce their earnings.
Illegal fishing can continue despite government rules. Example: Some fishermen may
secretly catch fish during a ban.
High demand for fish can encourage overfishing. Example: More seafood demand can
lead fishermen to catch more fish.
Lack of awareness among fishermen can make sustainable fishing difficult. Example:
Some fishermen may not know the importance of allowing young fish to grow.

BASIC DEFINITIONS
Cultivation: Preparing the land and growing crops.
Ploughing: Turning and loosening the soil using a plough before planting seeds.
Irrigation: Supplying water to crops artificially when there is not enough rainfall.
Weeding: Removing unwanted plants (weeds) that grow among crops.
Fertilizer: Substances added to the soil to provide nutrients and help crops grow
better.
Pesticides: Chemicals used to control or kill pests that damage crops.
Insecticides: Chemicals specifically used to kill harmful insects that attack crops.
HYV (High Yielding Variety Seeds): Seeds specially developed to produce more
crops than traditional seeds.
GM Seeds (Genetically Modified Seeds): Seeds whose genes have been changed
to give them useful characteristics, such as resistance to pests or diseases.
Harvesting: Cutting and collecting mature crops from the fields.
Threshing: Separating the grain from the stalks and husks after harvesting.

WHY AGRICULTURAL LAND IS NO LONGER PRODUCING
CROPS IN MANY REGIONS OF PAKISTAN?
Water logging – over-irrigation or unlined canals which cause seepage of water into the
ground causing a rise in water table to the surface making land uncultivable.
Salinity – salts rise with water table and are left on the surface when water evaporates
making land barren and uncultivable.
Overgrazing – too many livestock animals in too small an area has caused soil erosion.
Over cultivation – crops are not rotated or too little fertilizer and soil becomes infertile.
Exhausted Floods – top soil washed away by floods make it unfit for crops.
Drought – land becomes too dry to support crops.
Alternative use Large part of land is used for housing and industrial projects.
Land fragmentation – farming becomes inefficient Zamindari system of Landlords – no
incentive for farmers Workforce migrates to urban areas so lack of skilled or unskilled
workers – no one to work the land.
Siltation in reservoirs therefore reduces availability of irrigation water.

POULTRY FARMING
Poultry farming is a significant contributor to Pakistan’s economy,
providing employment to millions of people and playing a crucial role
in food security.
Poultry products, especially chicken meat and eggs, are essential
sources of affordable protein for the Pakistani population.
The poultry industry generates employment across its value chain,
including feed production, hatcheries, farms, processing plants, and
marketing.
Poultry farming is closely linked with other agricultural sectors. It
supports crop farming through the use of poultry manure as organic
fertilizer, enhancing soil fertility and crop yields.
CHALLENGES
One of the major challenges faced by poultry farmers is the outbreak
of diseases such as avian influenza and Newcastle disease.
The rising cost of poultry feed, which is largely dependent on imports,
affects the profitability of poultry farming.
Limited access to technical education and training hinders farmers'
ability to implement best practices in poultry management, feeding,
and disease control, reducing overall efficiency and productivity.

GAS EXTRACTION
1. Derrick: It supports the drilling equipment and helps lower and raise the drill pipe into the ground.
2. Travelling Block: It moves up and down to lift or lower the drilling equipment.
3. Top Drive: It rotates the drill pipe, which turns the drill bit at the bottom and breaks the rocks
underground.
4. Drilling Fluid Hose: It carries drilling fluid from the pumping system into the drill pipe.
5. Drill Pipe: It carries drilling fluid down to the drill bit and transmits rotation to the bit to drill
through the rocks.
6. Drilling Fluid: It cools and lubricates the drill bit and carries broken rock particles back to the
surface through the space around the drill pipe.
7. Casing: It is a strong pipe installed inside the drilled hole to prevent the well from collapsing and to
protect groundwater from contamination.
8. Blowout Preventer (BOP): It seals the well when necessary to control unexpected pressure and
prevent oil, gas or drilling fluid from escaping uncontrollably.
9. Tubing: After drilling and preparing the well for production, tubing is installed to carry oil or gas
from underground to the surface.
The drilling rig rotates a drill bit to break underground rocks and create a well. Drilling fluid removes
rock particles, casing supports the well, and the blowout preventer helps control pressure. Once the
well is ready for production, tubing carries oil or gas to the surface.

DRY PORT
A dry port is an inland facility where goods are stored, processed, and cleared for customs,
just like at a seaport, but it is located away from the coast.
WORKING OF DRY PORTS:
Dry ports are located in cities or areas away from the sea, such as Lahore,
Faisalabad, and Peshawar. This reduces the need to travel all the way to Karachi or
Gwadar for trade.
At a dry port, customs officials inspect and clear goods for import or export. This
means traders don’t need to go to the main sea port for paperwork.
Goods are transported to and from dry ports using trains or trucks. For example,
items arriving by ship in Karachi can be sent to Lahore’s dry port for further
processing.
Dry ports have warehouses to store goods safely until they are cleared or
transported.
These ports provide all the services needed for trade, like weighing goods,
packaging, and issuing transport documents.
REQUIREMENT FOR THE CONSTRUCTIONS OF DRY PORTS:
The dry port should be built near industrial areas, highways, or railways to make it
easy to move goods to and from seaports and factories.
A big piece of land is needed to store goods, park trucks, and set up warehouses
and offices.
Good connections to railways and roads are essential to move goods efficiently
between the dry port and other locations.
The dry port must have customs offices to check and clear goods for import and
export.
Cranes, forklifts, and other equipment are necessary to load, unload, and move
goods efficiently.

HE REIMPOSED JIZYA TAX !
Jizya was a special tax taken from non-Muslims living in the Mughal Empire.
It was charged in return for protection provided by the government and army.
Non-Muslims were allowed to practice their religion freely after paying this tax.
Muslims did not pay Jizya because they already paid Islamic taxes like Zakat.
Q. Why did Hindus resist paying the Jizya Tax?
Firstly, Hindus resisted paying the Jizya Tax because they felt it was unfair to charge non￾Muslims only because of their religion. This tax made many Hindus feel insulted and treated as
second-class citizens. Aurangzeb re-imposed the Jizya Tax in 1679 on all non-Muslims in the
Mughal Empire. This shows that religious policies of Aurangzeb increased anger among Hindus
and created opposition against Mughal rule.
Secondly, the Jizya Tax created an extra financial burden on poor people. Farmers, traders,
and workers already paid many taxes, so another tax made their lives more difficult. The tax
had to be paid regularly by non-Muslims, which affected poor Hindus the most. This proves
that economic pressure caused dissatisfaction and they resisted Jizya Tax.
Thirdly, Hindus believed Aurangzeb was trying to reduce their importance in society. The tax
increased divisions between Muslims and Hindus and damaged unity in the empire. Many
Hindu leaders, including Rajputs and Marathas, opposed Aurangzeb’s policies after the tax
was reimposed. This further became a reason why Jizya tax was oppossed by Hindus.

WHY CLIVE WON AT PLESSEY?
Firstly, Clive made secret agreements with important Bengal nobles, most importantly Mir
Jafar, promising them money and power if they did not support Nawab Siraj-ud-Daula in
battle. At the crucial moment many of the Nawab’s commanders either stayed inactive or
switched sides. The Nawab’s large army lost unity and fighting strength. This internal
betrayal helped the clive to defeat the Siraj’s force.
Secondly, Clive had better-trained and more disciplined soldiers than the Nawab's army.
During the battle, heavy rain made the Nawab's gunpowder and ammunition wet, as they
were not properly protected. As a result, much of the Nawab's artillery could not be used
effectively. However, the British had protected their gunpowder from the rain, so their
weapons continued to work. Clive was therefore able to use his artillery effectively and
this helped Clive defeat the larger army of Siraj-ud-Daula.
Thirdly, Clive also carefully chose his position near the mango grove at Plassey, which gave
his troops some protection from enemy fire. He waited for the right opportunity and
attacked when the Nawab's army became confused and weakened. Therefore, Clive's
careful preparation, knowledge of the enemy and good timing helped him defeat the
much larger army of Siraj-ud-Daula.

Q. Why Haji Shariatullah started his Faraizi Movement?
The reformers believed that Muslims had become weak because they had moved away from
the true teachings of Islam. Their aim was to guide Muslims back to the Quran and the Sunnah
of Prophet Muhammad صلى الله عليه وسلم so that they could strengthen their faith, improve their religious
practices, and regain the glory they had enjoyed in the past.
The reformers believed that many customs and beliefs had entered Muslim society which were
not part of Islam. Their aim was to purify Islam by encouraging Muslims to abandon these un￾Islamic practices and follow only those teachings that were based on the Quran and Sunnah.
They believed this would unite Muslims and strengthen the Muslim community.
Shah Waliullah believed that conflicts between Shias and Sunnis were weakening the Muslim
community at a time when the Mughal Empire was declining. Shah Waliullah believed that
Muslim unity was essential for restoring the strength and political power of Muslims in the
Subcontinent. By promoting harmony between the two sects, he hoped to create a stronger
and more united Muslim community capable of facing internal and external challenges.

Q. Why Jihad movement of Syed Ahmed Shaheed couldn’t succeed?
Firstly, many Muslims did not fully support Syed Ahmed Shaheed. Some groups were
influenced by local chiefs and were not willing to fight against the Sikhs. Even within his
followers, there were disagreements about leadership and methods of struggle. Without unity,
his movement could not gather enough strength to defeat powerful enemies. This shows the
movement failed because divided Muslims could not work together for a common cause.
Secondly, Some local Pathan leaders and tribal chiefs betrayed Syed Ahmed Shaheed by
siding with the Sikhs for their own personal interests. In key battles, they refused to help or
secretly informed the enemy about his plans. This betrayal weakened the Jihad Movement at
crucial moments, leading to military defeats. The lack of loyal support caused his movement
to collapse.
Thirdly, The Sikh ruler, Maharaja Ranjit Singh, had a powerful and well-trained army equipped
with modern weapons. In contrast, Syed Ahmed Shaheed’s forces were poorly armed and
lacked resources. The Sikhs also used strict control to suppress the movement. His forces
could not match the military power of the Sikhs, and Syed Ahmed was eventually martyred in
1831 at the Battle of Balakot. This shows the superior strength of the Sikhs was a key reason
for the failure of his Jihad Movement.
Q. How Titu Mir protected the interest the Bengali Muslims?
Firstly, Titu Mir guided Bengali Muslims to follow true Islamic practices and leave un-Islamic
customs. He spread religious awareness and emphasized unity among Muslims so they could
live with dignity. This gave Muslims a strong religious identity and moral strength to resist
oppression. By reviving Islamic teachings, Titu Mir protected the faith and culture of Bengali
Muslims.
Secondly, Hindu landlords in Bengal forced Muslims to pay unfair taxes, such as the beard tax,
which targeted Islamic practices. Titu Mir openly opposed these taxes and led movements
against the landlords’ cruelty. His resistance gave relief to many poor Muslim peasants and
restored their confidence. By fighting against unjust taxes, he protected the economic and
religious interests of Muslims..
Thirdly, Titu Mir did not only rely on preaching; he also organized an army of peasants to resist
both the British rulers and Hindu landlords. He built a bamboo fort near Calcutta to defend
Muslims from attacks. Although he was killed in 1831, his bravery inspired future generations of
Muslims to resist oppression. By taking practical steps through armed resistance, he
safeguarded the rights and honor of Bengali Muslims.

Traditional cotton and handicraft workers lost their jobs

British policies favoured British traders and

Q. Why Urdu was chosen as the national language of Pakistan?
R1: Urdu was already understood by Muslims in many parts of India – helped unite
Muslims during the freedom movement – used in religious, educational, and political
writings – therefore became a symbol of Muslim identity and unity.
R2: Urdu had a strong Islamic and cultural background – poets like Allama Iqbal and
Mirza Ghalib wrote in Urdu – carried Islamic values and traditions – therefore matched
the ideology and culture of Pakistan.
R3: Urdu was not the language of any one province – acted as a neutral language
between Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa – helped connect all
regions under one identity – therefore promoted national unity and equality.
Q. Why have regional languages been promoted by the Pakistani
 government between 1947 and 1999?
R1: Pakistan had many regional languages like Punjabi, Sindhi, Balochi, and Pashto –
promoting them helped protect local cultures, traditions, and heritage – therefore
preserved Pakistan’s cultural diversity.
R2: People felt respected when their languages were recognized – reduced feelings of
neglect among smaller provinces and ethnic groups – therefore strengthened national
unity and reduced provincial differences.
R3: Regional languages made education and communication easier at the local level –
textbooks and radio programs could be understood more easily in mother tongues –
therefore improved literacy and spread awareness across Pakistan.

Muslim League
Formed in:
The All India Muslim League was formed
in 1906 at Dhaka under the leadership
of Nawab Salimullah and Agha Khan.
Achievements:
The League aimed to promote loyalty to
the British and safeguard Muslim
political interests.
It demanded separate electorates and
fair government jobs for Muslims.
Later, it became the main political
party leading the Pakistan Movement.
Indian National Congress
Formed in:
The Indian National Congress was
founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume, a British
officer.
Achievements:
It gave educated Indians a platform to
discuss political problems.
At first, it worked peacefully by sending
petitions to the British government.
Later, it became more aggressive and
started demanding full independence.
Over time, it came to represent mostly
Hindu interests, worrying Muslims.
WHY INC WAS FORMED?
Firstly, Many educated Indians felt that there was no proper organization through which
they could communicate their problems, opinions and demands to the British government.
They wanted an organised way to communicate their concerns to the British government.
Therefore, The INC was formed in 1885 to provide a platform where educated Indians
could discuss these issues and present them to the British authorities.
Secondly, India was divided by religion, language, caste and region, and people from
different areas did not always work together. There was a need to bring educated Indians
from different parts of the country together so they could discuss common problems and
develop a sense of national unity. Therefore, the INC was formed to bring Indians together
and encourage them to work for common political interests.
Thirdly, By the 1880s, many educated Indians were becoming unhappy with British
policies. They wanted a peaceful and constitutional way for them to express their
dissatisfaction through meetings, discussions and petitions instead of using violence.
Therefore, the INC was formed to provide a peaceful way for Indians to express their
political dissatisfaction and demands.

support.

Background:
These reforms were introduced in 1909 through Indian Council Act.
These reforms were combined efforts of John Morley - the Secretary of State for India
and Lord Minto - the Viceroy of India.
Features:
The number of members in the Central Legislative Council increased from 16 to 60.
The number of members in the Provincial Legislatures was also increased:
50 members in Bengal, Madras and Bombay.
30 members in smaller provinces.
Muslims were given the right to elect their own representatives. This was called
separate electorates.
Members of the Legislative Councils could discuss the budget, suggest changes and vote
on it.
Two Indians were allowed to join the Council of the Secretary of State for India.
The Governor-General could appoint one Indian to his Executive Council.
Outcome:
These reforms were opposed by Indian National Congress.
Morley Minto Reform
WHY CAME?
Fistly, After the Partition of Bengal in 1905, both Hindus and Muslims started demanding
more political rights. The British feared these protests could turn violent. British wanted to
calm down the growing political unrest in India so they introduced the reforms.
Secondly, After the Simla Deputation of 1906, the British realized Muslims were loyal and
cooperative. British wanted to reward loyal communities so they introduced the reforms to
give relaxation to those communities especially Muslims.
Thirdly, The British wanted to improve their image after years of criticism. They wanted to
allow some Indians to become members of Legislative Councils which will show British
were promoting political progress and modernization. So they introduced reforms.
WHY OPPOSED?
Fistly, Indians were allowed to join the Legislative Councils, they had no real authority to
make or change laws. Most decisions were still controlled by the British officials. Congress
felt that these reforms were only a show and did not bring true self-government. This is
why Congress rejected them as meaningless and unfair.
Secondly, Another reason for opposition was the introduction of separate electorates for
Muslims. Congress believed this step would divide Indians on religious lines and weaken
their unity against British rule. They argued that the British were using the policy of “divide
and rule” to keep Hindus and Muslims apart.
Thirdly, The Indian National Congress wanted larger councils so more Indians could join
governance, but the British only made limited changes. They had no plan to give real
power or introduce democracy in India.

Background:
The reforms were prepared together by John Montague (the Secretary of State) and
Lord Chelmsford (the Viceroy).
Features:
The Central Legislature had 2 houses: Upper House and Lower House.
The Upper House had 60 members and the Lower House had 144 members.
The Upper House worked for 5 years and the Lower House worked for 3 years.
Some powers were given to the Central Government and some to the Provincial
Governments.
Diarchy was introduced in the provinces, which means provincial government was
divided into two parts.
The Executive Council did not have to answer to the Legislature.
Provincial Legislatures had only one house.
New reforms were to be made after 10 years.
Outcome:
However, Indians were unhappy because the British still held most authority.
Montague Chelmsford Reform
WHY CAME?
Firstly, After World War I, Indians expected political rewards for their support during the
war. The British feared more protests and unrest if they ignored these demands. British
wanted to calm down the growing demand for self-government in India. Therefore, the
reforms were introduced.
Secondly, The British government wanted to prove to the world that it was modern and
fair, especially after the war. By giving Indians limited powers in provinces, they tried to
show progress toward self-rule. Thus, the reforms were introduced to improve Britain’s
image.
Thirdly, The British also wanted to train Indians for future administration through a system
called dyarchy, some subjects were given to Indian ministers, while important areas like
remained under British control. Therefore, the reforms were introduced to create
controlled participation without losing British authority.
WHY OPPOSED?
Firstly, British gave very limited powers to Indians. Although Indians were included in
provincial governments, all major decisions were still controlled by the British governors.
The British officials could overrule Indian ministers anytime.
Secondly, Under the system of Dyarchy, subjects were divided into “transferred” and
“reserved” categories, where Indians handled minor departments like education, while the
British kept control over important ones like finance and police. This made Indians feel
humiliated and powerless.
Thirdly, during World War I Indians had supported the British in the war, hoping for greater
political freedom in return. But when the reforms came, they were slow, limited, and
disappointing. Many leaders felt betrayed by British promises of self-rule.

reduced.

It marked the success of Turkish nationalists and ended the Khilafat Movement in
India.

Background:
In 1927, the Conservative British government sent a 7-member commission led by Sir
John Simon to suggest constitutional reforms for India.
Features:
The commission recommended a federal system of government.
The System of Diarchy ended.
The commission also recommended a federal system of government, ending diarchy,
and abolishing separate electorates for Muslims.
However, it did not give Muslims one-third representation in the central government
and also refused to make Sindh and the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) separate
provinces.
Outcome:
Because of these recommendations, both the Indian National Congress and the All￾India Muslim League rejected the report.
Simon Commission
WHY CAME?
Firstly, The British government wanted to study whether Indians were ready for more
political power and self-government. The commission was supposed to suggest changes
for better administration. It was a step to plan the next constitutional reforms for India.
Secondly, Many protests and movements were taking place against British rule. The British
government wanted to calm the situation by showing that it cared about India’s political
future. By sending the commission, they hoped to reduce public anger and delay the
demand for full freedom.
Thirdly, British wanted to keep full control over the reform process. They did not trust
Indian leaders to make constitutional changes themselves. By forming a commission with
only British members, they ensured that the decisions would favor their interests.
WHY OPPOSED?
Firstly, All seven members of the commission were British, which deeply offended the
Indian people. They believed that Indians were capable of discussing their own political
future.
Secondly, The British had promised more participation after World War I, but the
commission gave no sign of real independence. Instead, it showed that the British wanted
to continue ruling India.
Thirdly, The British made all the decisions in London without asking Indian leaders about
their opinions or needs. This made people feel insulted and ignored in matters that directly
affected their country.

Background:
Muhammad Ali Jinnah called the All Muslim Party Conference in Delhi on 20 March 1927
and chaired the meeting.
The purpose was to protect the political rights of Muslims and improve relations with
the Indian National Congress.
The conference proposed that:
Sindh should become a separate province.
The North-West Frontier Province (NWFP) and Balochistan should be given the status of
provinces.
Muslims should get one-third of the seats in the Central Legislative Assembly.
In return, the All-India Muslim League was willing to give up its demand for separate
electorates if these proposals were accepted.
Outcome:
These proposals later became part of Jinnah's Fourteen Points.
Delhi Proposals
WHY PRESENTED BY ML?
Firstly, The Muslim League presented the Delhi Proposals in 1927 to show its willingness to
cooperate with the Indian National Congress for constitutional reforms. Muslim leaders
wanted to prove that they were ready to work together for India’s self-government.
Secondly, Another reason was fear of majority domination as Congress grew stronger, so
Muslim leaders wanted firm safeguards. By presenting the Delhi Proposals they aimed to
fix these protections before any new constitution was made. .
Thirdly, Since many Congress leaders had started opposing separate electorates, Muslims
felt the need for a new understanding. By offering fresh terms, they tried to keep political
dialogue open between both communities.

WHY RTCS CONDUCTED?
Firstly, The Round Table Conferences were held because the Simon Commission of 1927
did not include any Indians, which made Indians angry. Indians wanted their views to be
heard in making new laws. The British understood that they needed Indian leaders’ support
for future plans to work. So, they arranged meetings to discuss India’s political future with
them.
Secondly, The Civil Disobedience Movement and other protests showed Indians would not
accept British rule without change. The British wanted to reduce tension and bring peace.
So, they arranged meetings to discuss a new political system.
Thirdly, Hindus, Muslims, and other groups disagreed over political rights and
representation. The British wanted all communities to work together on a common plan.
Leaders like Jinnah and Gandhi were invited to share their opinions. These conferences
aimed to create unity and make a political plan that included everyone.
WHY RTCS COULDN’T ACHIEVE SUCCESS?
Firstly, The Round Table Conferences failed because the Congress Party did not attend
the First Conference in 1930. Since the Congress was the largest political party in India, its
absence made the discussions one-sided and incomplete. Without Congress participation,
no major decisions could represent all Indians. This weakened the conference from the
start. Therefore, the absence of Congress was a major reason why the Round Table
Conferences could not achieve success.
Secondly, The Muslim League, Hindu Mahasabha, Sikhs, and other minorities all had
different demands and could not agree on key constitutional issues. This disagreement
made it impossible to present a single Indian viewpoint. The British took advantage of
these divisions and delayed reforms. Hence, internal disunity among Indian leaders led to
the failure of the Round Table Conferences.
Thirdly, Instead of accepting Indian demands for self-rule, they continued to control major
areas like defense and finance. Even Gandhi’s efforts in the Second Conference could not
change their attitude. The British only wanted limited reforms to maintain control over
India. Therefore, the Round Table Conferences failed as the British were unwilling to share
genuine political power.

Background:
After a long evaluation and analysis of Simon commission, INC and ML demands and
RTCs, the British Parliament passed the Government of India Act in 1935.
Features:
Provinces were given more power and elected ministers could run provincial
governments.
It proposed a federation of British Indian provinces and princely states (though this
federation was never fully implemented).
Some provinces were given two houses of legislature.
The system of separate electorates for different communities continued.
Governors still had special powers and could overrule elected ministers in some
situations.
25% increase in the voting rights to the Indians.
Outcome:
The Act was partly accepted and partly rejected by Indian political parties.
Government Act of India 1935
WHY IMPORTANT?
Firstly, For the first time, Indian ministers were allowed to form governments and make
decisions in their own provinces. This gave Indians practical experience in running
administration and politics.
Secondly, It planned to unite the provinces and princely states under one central
government. Although the federal part was never fully applied, it showed a step toward
forming a united Indian constitution.
Thirdly, The number of Indian voters increased to about 35 million, allowing more people to
take part in elections. This gave Indians a greater sense of responsibility and involvement
in politics.
WHY OPPOSED?
Firstly, Even though provincial governments were formed, the British governors could
dismiss ministers and reject laws anytime. This meant Indian leaders had no real authority
in their own provinces.
Secondly, Important areas like defense, finance, and foreign affairs were not given to
Indian ministers. The British used these powers to interfere in every major decision. Indians
realized that the Act was only a way to continue British dominance.
Thirdly, only a few rich people could vote due to strict property qualifications. Most
ordinary Indians were too poor to meet these conditions, so they were excluded from the
elections. This made the government unrepresentative and unfair.

Elections in India
WHY ML COULD’NT PERFORM WELL?
Firstly, The League had limited membership, fewer offices, and lacked strong leadership in
many provinces. Most Muslims were not aware of its aims and did not actively support it.
On the other hand, the Congress was well-organized and popular among the people.
Secondly, Congress had more resources, better election campaigns, and strong local
leaders who influenced the voters. Many Muslims also voted for Congress candidates,
believing they would protect their interests. This made it difficult for the Muslim League to
compete effectively.
Thirdly, Muslim League also failed because it did not focus on the problems of ordinary
Muslims. Its message was more about elite politics rather than social and economic issues
that affected common people. Many Muslims felt the League did not represent their daily
struggles.

WORLD WAR II STARTED
September 1, 1939, to September 2, 1945
Note: Congress resigned from ministries in 1939.
WHY CONGRESS RESIGNED FROM MINISTRIES
Firstly, The Viceroy declared India’s participation in the war against Germany on his own.
Congress felt disrespected since they were not consulted on such an important matter.
This proved that the British still held real control over India. So, Congress quit in protest
against this unfair and undemocratic decision.
Secondly, When World War II started, Congress asked the British to promise self-rule
(Swaraj) in return for India’s help. But the British refused to give any such promise. This
made Congress realize that the British didn’t plan to end their control. So, Congress
resigned to show they wouldn’t support the war without freedom.
Thirdly, By quitting the ministries, they wanted to create problems for the British during
the war. They believed this would force the British to talk and offer more political rights. It
was also a way to show unity and strength among Indian leaders. So, Congress resigned in
1939 as a strategy to push for independence.
The Day of Deliverance was observed on 22nd December 1939 by Muslims in India, led
by Quaid-e Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah.
It was celebrated after the Congress ministries resigned from all provinces when Britain
declared India’s participation in World War II without consulting Indian leaders.
Jinnah declared this day as a mark of relief from Congress’s oppressive rule during
1937–39.
Muslims held meetings and thanked Allah for their freedom from Congress domination.
The event strengthened the Muslim League’s position as the true representative of
Indian Muslims.

Background:
The Lahore Resolution was passed on 23rd March
1940 during the All India Muslim League session at
Minto Park, Lahore, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah &
presented by Maulvi AK Fazal ul Haq.
Features:
It demanded independent states for Muslims in the
north western and eastern parts of India where
they were in majority.
The resolution gave a clear goal of a separate
homeland, later known as Pakistan Resolution.
Outcome:
It united Muslims under one demand and gave new
direction to their struggle. This became the
foundation of Pakistan’s creation in 1947.
Lahore Resolution
WHY MUSLIMS DEMANDED FOR SEPARATE HOMELAND?
Firstly, Muslims demanded a separate homeland in 1940 because Congress rule from 1937
to 1939 showed clear Hindu bias. Muslims were forced to sing Bande Mataram, their
religion was disrespected, and Urdu was discouraged. These unfair actions made Muslims
feel like second-class citizens under Hindu control. Therefore, they wanted a separate
homeland where their religion and rights would be safe.
Secondly, Another reason for demanding a separate homeland was the Nehru Report of
1928, which ignored Muslim rights. It rejected separate electorates and reduced Muslim
representation in politics. The report seemed to favor a Hindu-majority India with little
space for Muslims. This made Muslims feel insecure and betrayed. So, they started
demanding a separate homeland to protect their political identity and rights.
Thirdly, Gandhi’s stubborn attitude in the Second Round Table Conference also increased
Muslim support for separation. He refused to accept the Muslim League’s demand for
separate electorates and ignored their concerns. This showed that Congress was not ready
to share power fairly. As a result, Muslims lost trust in Hindu leaders and believed only a
separate homeland could ensure their safety and freedom.

Cripps Mission Plan
Background: The Cripps Mission came to India in
March 1942 under Sir Stafford Cripps, sent by Britain
to get Indian support in World War II.
Detail:
After World War II, India would be given Dominion
Status.
Indians would form a Constituent Assembly to
make a new constitution for India.
Any province could refuse to join the new union
and could make its own constitution.
Outcome:
The Congress rejected it demanding complete
independence, while the Muslim League did not
accept it without Muslim safeguards
WHY REJECTED BY INDIANS?
Firstly, The Cripps Mission was rejected because it did not offer immediate independence.
The British only promised freedom after World War II, which disappointed both Congress
and the Muslim League. Indians wanted a fixed date and clear plan for independence, not
just future promises. This showed the British were not serious about ending their rule. So,
Indians rejected the proposal as useless.
Secondly, The Muslim League also rejected the Cripps Mission because it did not clearly
accept the demand for Pakistan. Although it allowed provinces some freedom, it did not
ensure a separate homeland for Muslims. Jinnah and the League felt the plan ignored
Muslim unity and rights. Therefore, they rejected it since it failed to meet their goal of
creating an independent Muslim state.
Thirdly, Another reason for rejection was that the plan allowed provinces or states to stay
out of the Indian federation if they wanted. Congress opposed this because it could divide
India and make it weak. They wanted one united and strong central government. This idea
of separation caused disagreement. So, Congress rejected the plan as it encouraged
division instead of unity.

Quit India Resolution
WHY INC STARTED IT?
Firstly, Indians were angry that the British were using India’s resources in the war without their consent.
Congress wanted the British to leave so Indians could make their own decisions. The Cripps Mission had
already failed to satisfy them. Therefore, Congress demanded the British to “Quit India” and give
immediate independence.
Secondly, The British had often promised reforms and independence after the war, but never fulfilled them.
Congress leaders believed these were just tricks to delay freedom again. They thought only a strong
movement could force the British to act. Hence, the Quit India Resolution was passed to pressure the
British to leave India immediately.
Thirdly, Japan had already captured Burma and was moving closer to Indian borders. Indians feared that if
the British stayed in control, India would become a battlefield. Congress believed an independent India
could better protect itself. Therefore, the threat of Japanese invasion pushed Congress to demand the
British to leave India quickly.
Background: The Quit India Resolution was passed by
the Congress in August 1942 in Bombay, led by
Mahatma Gandhi.
Detail:
The Congress demanded that the British must leave
India immediately.
After the British left, Indians would form their own
national government.
Jinnah, opposed the Quit India Movement because
they believed it was mainly for a united India and
ignored the demand for Pakistan.
Outcome:
The British responded by arresting all major Congress
leaders and using force to stop protests. It caused
much unrest across India.
WHY ML NOT JOINED IT?
Firstly, The League felt that Congress was again acting like it represented all Indians, which ignored
Muslim opinions. Muslims believed such a movement would only strengthen Hindu control. This created
mistrust between the two communities. Therefore, the League stayed away from the movement as it did
not protect Muslim interests.
Secondly, The League thought cooperating with the British would help Muslims gain political benefits
after the war. Jinnah believed that supporting the British would make them recognize Muslims as a
separate nation. Joining Congress’s movement would destroy this understanding. So, the League refused
to take part in the Quit India Movement.
Thirdly, The League was focused on getting a separate homeland for Muslims, while Congress wanted one
united India. If the British left immediately, power would go to Congress, and Muslims would again be
under Hindu rule. To avoid this risk, the League opposed the movement. Thus, it did not support Quit India
to protect Muslim political goals.

Gandhi Jinnah Talk
WHY GANDHI JINNAH TALK FAILED?
Firstly, Gandhi wanted a unitary form of government with all powers in the hands of one
central authority. However, Jinnah wanted a federal system, where provinces especially
Muslim majority areas would have more control over their own affairs. Jinnah feared that a
unitary system would lead to Hindu domination. Therefore, the talks failed as both leaders
could not agree on how power should be shared in India.
Secondly, Another reason for the failure was that Gandhi claimed to represent all Indians,
including Muslims. Jinnah strongly disagreed, saying that the Congress only spoke for Hindus
and not for Muslims. He argued that the Muslim League was the only true representative of
the Muslims of India. Gandhi’s refusal to accept this angered Jinnah and created more
distance between them. Hence, the talks failed because Gandhi did not accept the League’s
political authority over Muslims.
Thirdly, Gandhi completely rejected the Two-Nation Theory. Jinnah believed that Hindus and
Muslims were two separate nations with different cultures and religions, and could not live
under one government. Gandhi opposed this idea, saying both communities were part of one
Indian nation. This became the biggest point of disagreement between them. Therefore, the
Gandhi–Jinnah Talks failed as Gandhi refused to accept the Muslim demand for a separate
homeland.
Background: The Gandhi–Jinnah Talks took place in
September 1944 at Jinnah’s residence in Bombay to
find a political solution for India’s future.
Detail:
He suggested that India should first get
independence from the British, then the future
system could be decided.
Gandhi considered himself as a spokesperson on
the behalf Indians.
Gandhi wanted all the powers to the center
instead of provinces
Also, he rejected the concept of two-nation
theory.
Outcome:
Jinnah rejected all these demands of Gandhi.

Simla Conference
WHY CONFERENCE FAILED?
Firstly, Congress and the Muslim League claimed to represent Indian Muslims. Congress said it
represented all communities of India, including Muslims, while the League argued that only it
had the right to speak for Muslims. Jinnah insisted that Muslim representatives must be
chosen from the League only. Congress refused to accept this demand. Therefore, the
conference failed because both parties could not agree on Muslim representation.
Secondly, Another reason was the British wanted to include both Congress and League
members in the new government. However, Jinnah demanded that all Muslim seats in the
Council should be given to League nominees only. Congress opposed this and wanted to
include some non-League Muslims. This created a deadlock between the two sides. Hence, the
Simla Conference ended without any final agreement.
Thirdly, The Simla Conference also failed because there was a lack of trust between the
Congress and the Muslim League. Jinnah believed that Congress would use its power to
dominate Muslims if it entered the government. On the other hand, Congress thought Jinnah
was trying to divide India. Both sides focused on protecting their own interests instead of
cooperating. Therefore, the conference failed as mutual mistrust stopped any chance of
agreement.
Background: The Simla Conference was held in
June–July 1945 under the British Viceroy Lord
Wavell at Simla.
Detail:
The aim was to form a new Executive Council in
India with equal representation for Hindus and
Muslims.
The Muslim League demanded that only it should
nominate all Muslim members, but Congress
disagreed.
Due to this disagreement, the conference failed.
Outcome:
Its failure made it clear that cooperation between
Congress and Muslim League was no longer possible.

Cabinet Mission Plan
WHY PLAN FAILED?
Firstly, Congress and the Muslim League disagreed on the grouping of provinces. The plan
suggested that Muslim-majority and Hindu-majority provinces should form separate groups
within one Indian Union. The League supported this idea as it gave Muslims some
independence, but Congress opposed it, fearing it would lead to Pakistan later. This
disagreement created a serious conflict. Therefore, the plan failed as both parties could not
agree on the grouping system.
Secondly, Another reason for the failure was that the Congress rejected the idea of limited
central powers. The plan wanted the central government to handle only defense, foreign
affairs, and communication, while provinces would control the rest. Congress wanted a strong
central government with full authority over all matters. The League, however, wanted more
provincial autonomy to protect Muslim interests. Hence, this clash over power sharing led to
the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Thirdly, The Cabinet Mission Plan also failed because the trust between Congress and the
Muslim League completely broke down. Jinnah felt that Congress would never honestly share
power with Muslims, while Congress believed that Jinnah only wanted to create Pakistan. Both
parties began preparing for separate political futures instead of compromise. This deep
mistrust made cooperation impossible. Therefore, the Cabinet Mission Plan failed as neither
side was willing to work together.

Why Direct Action Day was a turning
point for the partition of India
Firstly, When the Muslim League called for Direct Action, serious riots broke out in Calcutta
and other cities. Thousands of people were killed, and trust between the two communities
was destroyed. These events proved that unity between Hindus and Muslims was
impossible. Therefore, Direct Action Day made the demand for partition stronger and more
urgent.
Secondly, The League proved that it had the full support of Indian Muslims for the creation
of Pakistan. The massive participation in protests made it clear to the British and Congress
that Muslims were ready to fight for their separate homeland. It became difficult to ignore
their demand after this event. Hence, Direct Action Day became a key step toward the
partition of India.
Thirdly, The widespread violence and tension made them realize that keeping India united
would lead to more bloodshed. The failure of all earlier negotiations and the chaos of
Direct-Action Day forced the British to speed up their plans for independence. Therefore,
this event directly pushed the British toward accepting the idea of dividing India into two
countries.

Lord Mountbatten, the last British Viceroy, on 3rd
June 1947.

It clearly accepted the partition of India into two
independent states, India and Pakistan.
Provinces like Punjab and Bengal were to be
divided based on religious majority, and
referendums were held in NWFP to decide their
future.

the plan.
Outcome:
This plan finally led to the creation of Pakistan on
14th August 1947

Radcliffe Award
Background: Sir Cyril Radcliffe was a British lawyer
who was sent to India in June 1947 to draw the
boundary line between India and Pakistan..
Detail:
He had no prior knowledge of Indian geography
or culture, yet he had to complete his work
within five weeks.
He led the Boundary Commission, dividing
Punjab and Bengal based on religious
majorities.
His decisions left many people unhappy and
caused mass migration and violence.
Outcome:
The Radcliffe Line became the official border
between India and Pakistan.
Why Redcliff Award was criticized in
Pakistan?
Firstly, Districts like Gurdaspur and Ferozepur, which had a large number of Muslims, were
handed over to India. This decision was seen as biased and against the spirit of partition. It
also gave India a road link to Kashmir, which later caused serious conflict. Therefore,
Pakistan criticized the award for being unjust and favoring India.
Secondly, Sir Cyril Redcliff had never been to India before and did not understand the local
conditions. Because of this, many areas were divided unfairly, separating villages, families,
and even farmlands. The people suffered greatly as they were forced to leave their homes.
Hence, Pakistan criticized the award for being rushed and poorly planned.
Thirdly, Many important industries, irrigation canals, and railway lines went to India, leaving
Pakistan weak in its early days. The sudden border changes also caused chaos during
migration. These unfair decisions made Pakistan feel betrayed by the British. Therefore, the
Redcliff Award was strongly condemned as it damaged Pakistan’s stability from the very
beginning.

him for his strong knowledge of Islam and politics. Leaders believed he could guide the
community at a difficult time. His wisdom and status made him the best choice to lead the
session. Therefore, he was selected to chair the meeting due to his great respect among
Muslims.

poetry had already inspired them to stay united and strong. By choosing him as chairman,
the Muslim League wanted to motivate Muslims and remind them of their identity. Hence,

ideas for Muslim rights. He believed Muslims were a separate nation and needed their own
political power. At the session, he later presented the famous idea of a separate homeland
for Muslims. This became a turning point in history. Therefore, Iqbal was honored as
chairman because he was seen as the right leader to shape the future of Muslims in India.

separate Muslim homeland. In 1933, he wrote a pamphlet called Now or Never in which he
suggested the name Pakistan for the Muslim majority areas. This gave a clear identity and
a name to the idea of a separate country. Muslims now had a proper word to represent
their dream. Therefore, his role was significant because he introduced the name that later
became our nation.
Secondly, Another reason for his importance is that he explained the need for a separate
homeland in simple and strong words. Rehmat Ali warned that Muslims would lose their
rights and identity under Hindu control in a united India. He encouraged Muslims to think
independently and protect their future. His message helped many people understand why
separation was necessary. Hence, he played a key role in making Muslims aware of their
political rights.
Thirdly, Chaudhry Rehmat Ali was also significant because he inspired other leaders and
students to support the idea of Pakistan. His words spread quickly among young Muslims
studying in India and abroad, especially in Cambridge. Many of them later joined the
Pakistan Movement and worked for independence. His ideas helped strengthen the
movement from the start. Therefore, Rehmat Ali’s influence helped turn the dream of
Pakistan into a strong public demand.

Explanation / Detail:
Radcliffe drew borders through the Muslim￾majority provinces of Punjab and Bengal,
awarding some Muslim-majority districts to
India.
Ferozpur & Gurdaspur were Muslim majority
areas in Punjab but were given to India.
Nadia and Murshidabad areas was also Muslim
Majority in the east but given to India.
About 7–8 million refugees entered Pakistan
within months.
Many people had to live in temporary camps.
Linkback:
Pakistan was a new country with very limited
resources, so it became extremely difficult to
provide food, cloth, Shelter & Medicines led to the
serious refugee crisis.
Why did Pakistan face refugee crisis?
Firstly, After Partition in 1947, millions of Muslims migrated from India to Pakistan to live in a
Muslim homeland. This migration happened suddenly and without proper planning. Trains,
roads, and camps were overcrowded with refugees. Pakistan was a new country with limited
resources and weak administration. As a result, it became very difficult to manage food,
shelter, and transport for refugees.
Secondly, Large-scale Hindu-Muslim riots broke out in many areas of India after Partition.
Muslims faced killings, attacks, and destruction of their homes and property. Due to fear for
their lives, they were forced to leave their homes urgently. Many arrived in Pakistan injured,
homeless, and without belongings. This sudden inflow increased pressure on Pakistan’s weak
system.
Thirdly, At independence, Pakistan had no proper refugee camps or housing facilities. Major
cities like Lahore and Karachi were not ready for such a large population. There were
shortages of food, jobs, hospitals, and clean water. The government also lacked experienced
officers and financial resources. Therefore, managing millions of refugees became a serious
national crisis.

Economic Problem
Explanation / Detail:
At the time of the Partition of India, it was
decided that Pakistan would receive ₹750
million as its share of financial assets.
However, India delayed the payment, only ₹200
million was paid initially – Remaining ₹550
million was delayed.
Most industries (factories, mills, manufacturing
centers) were in India (Calcutta).
Pakistan faced severe shortage of money.
Government struggled in (Running daily affairs +
Paying salaries + managing administration).
Linkback:
Therefore, this delay created serious financial
problems for Pakistan at the very beginning.
Firstly, Pakistan was supposed to receive 750 million rupees, India delayed the payment and
released only a part of it initially. This caused serious financial shortages for the new state.
Pakistan had to set up its government, army, and administration without enough money. The
shortage of funds affected development, salaries, and daily government functioning. As a
result, Pakistan started its journey with a weak and unstable economy.
Secondly, Pakistan received mainly agricultural areas with very few industrial units. There
were shortages of machinery, skilled workers, and technical experts. Important industrial
cities like Bombay and Calcutta became part of India. This made Pakistan dependent on
imports for manufactured goods. Due to weak industrial development, the economy struggled
to grow in the early years.
Thirdly, The government had to spend a large part of its limited budget on refugee
rehabilitation. New cities, houses, and services had to be arranged quickly. At the same time,
Pakistan lacked trained officers and experienced administrators. This heavy financial burden
slowed economic stability. As a result, Pakistan faced serious economic pressure in its early
years.

Why Ayyub Khan shifted the capital
from Karachi to Islamabad?
Firstly, Ayub Khan shifted the capital from Karachi to Islamabad because Karachi was
located in the extreme south of Pakistan. It was very far from many other parts of the
country, especially the northern areas. Islamabad was chosen as it is in the center of the
country, which made it easier to connect and govern all regions.
Secondly, Karachi was a coastal city and was considered unsafe during war or foreign
attack because it could easily be targeted from the sea. Islamabad, on the other hand, is
surrounded by mountains and located inland, which made it a safer and more secure
place for the capital.
Thirdly, Karachi was already Pakistan’s biggest trade and business city. Keeping both
trade and government in the same city was causing overcrowding and administrative
problems. By shifting the capital to Islamabad, Ayub Khan wanted to separate the
government from commercial activities and allow Karachi to grow as the main economic
hub.
Why did Ayyub Khan fall from office?
Firstly, Ayub Khan fell from office because his political system, called “Basic
Democracies,
” was not truly democratic. People felt that they had no real voice in
choosing their leaders, and opposition parties strongly criticized his rule. This lack of
democracy reduced his popularity over time.
Secondly, Another reason was the economic situation. In the beginning, his policies
brought growth, but later the benefits went mostly to rich people and big industrialists.
Poor people felt ignored, and the gap between rich and poor widened. This caused unrest
among the public, especially students and workers.
Thirdly, the 1965 war with India also weakened Ayub Khan’s position. Although the
government claimed success, many Pakistanis felt disappointed with the outcome of the
Tashkent Agreement. Opposition leaders, especially Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, used this to turn
people against Ayub Khan. Facing protests, strikes, and pressure from all sides, Ayub
Khan resigned in 1969.

the Decade of Progress (1960–1969)? Explain your answer. [14] 
Question:
Pakistan’s relations with India:
During Ayub Khan’s rule (1958–1969), Pakistan’s relations with India began positively
but later turned hostile.
The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 was a major success, as it peacefully solved the river
water dispute.
However, tensions grew over Kashmir, and Pakistan’s closer ties with China made India
uneasy.
The 1965 war badly damaged relations, and although the Tashkent Agreement ended
the fighting, it left mistrust on both sides.
Despite one early success, Ayub Khan’s policy toward India mostly led to conflict and
long-term tension between the two countries.
Pakistan’s relations with USA:
Pakistan’s relations with the United States were close but mainly based on mutual
strategic interests.
Pakistan was the part of SEATO and CENTO alliances, gaining military and economic aid
from the U.S. in return for supporting it during the Cold War.
The U.S. helped Pakistan build industries, strengthen its military, and supported large
projects like dams under the Green Revolution.
However, the relationship weakened after the 1965 war with India, when the U.S.
suspended military assistance to both countries, leaving Pakistan disappointed and
feeling betrayed.
Relations with the U.S. helped Pakistan’s early economic and defense growth, they later
turned cold, showing that the friendship was based more on American interests than
long-term trust.
Pakistan’s relations with USSR:
Pakistan’s relations with the Soviet Union (USSR) were mostly tense and cautious.
At first, ties were poor because Pakistan was allied with the United States through
SEATO and CENTO, which the USSR viewed as unfriendly.
Tensions rose further after the 1960 U-2 plane incident, when an American spy plane
flying from Pakistan’s Peshawar airbase was shot down over Soviet territory, angering
the USSR.
However, relations improved slightly after the 1965 war with India, when the USSR
hosted the Tashkent Agreement to restore peace.
Although mistrust continued, the Tashkent peace efforts helped reduce some of the
tension between Pakistan and the Soviet Union.

Firstly, Bhutto’s industrial reforms could not succeed because the government took
control of too many industries without proper planning. Many experienced owners and
managers were removed, and government officers who replaced them did not have
enough skills to run the factories. This caused a drop in production and poor-quality goods.
Secondly, After seeing many factories being nationalized, investors became afraid that
their own businesses might also be taken away. Because of this fear, they stopped
investing in new industries. This reduced job opportunities and slowed down economic
growth in the country. Hence, the reforms failed because they discouraged private
investment and hurt Pakistan’s industrial progress.
Thirdly, Many appointments were made based on political connections instead of ability
or experience. This led to mismanagement, wastage of money, and weak decision-making.
Workers also became less motivated because they did not fear losing their jobs. Therefore,
the reforms did not succeed as corruption and poor management destroyed the purpose
of nationalization.

Pakistan’s relations with India were shaped by efforts to recover from the 1971 war and

Washington and strengthening ties with China and Muslim countries instead.

increased strain between the two nations.

showing Pakistan’s desire for greater independence in foreign policy.

period.

Sajjad Ali Shah was the Chief Justice of
Pakistan from 1994 to 1997.
He had conflicts with Prime Minister Nawaz
Sharif over the powers of the judiciary and the
government.
In 1997, the Supreme Court challenged Nawaz
Sharif’s actions, increasing tensions between
them.
The conflict weakened the relationship
between the government and the judiciary,
and Sajjad Ali Shah was eventually removed
from office in December 1997.

4 Mark Questions
Q1. Who were Mughals? [4]
Ans: The Mughals were a Muslim dynasty that ruled most of the Indian subcontinent from 1526 to 1857.They 
were originally Central Asian Turks and Mongols, descendants of Timur and Genghis Khan. The first Mughal 
ruler was Babur, who defeated Ibrahim Lodhi at the Battle of Panipat in 1526.They established a strong empire 
with famous rulers like Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, and Aurangzeb. The Mughal Empire declined in the 18th 
century and was later replaced by British rule.
Q. Who was Aurangzeb Alamgir? [4]
Ans: Aurangzeb was the sixth Mughal emperor who ruled India from 1658 to 1707. He was the son of Shah 
Jahan and received a strict Islamic education in his early life. Aurangzeb expanded the Mughal Empire to its 
greatest extent through wars and conquests. He was known for enforcing Islamic laws and banning some un￾Islamic practices. Aurangzeb died in 1707 at Ahmadnagar, marking the beginning of the Mughal Empire’s 
decline.
Q. Who was Shivaji Maharaj? [4]
Ans: Shivaji Maharaj was a famous Maratha leader born in 1630 at the Shivneri Fort in India. In his early life, 
he was inspired by his mother and teachers to fight against injustice. He built a strong army and established the 
Maratha Kingdom by defeating Mughal and local rulers. Shivaji is remembered for his bravery, good 
administration, and respect for all religions. He died in 1680 at Raigad Fort, leaving behind a powerful legacy 
for the Marathas.
Q. Who was Nawab Siraj ud Daula? [4]
Ans: Nawab Siraj ud Daula was the last independent Nawab of Bengal, born in 1733. In his early life, he was 
trained in military and administration under his grandfather Alivardi Khan. He became Nawab in 1756 and tried 
to resist the growing power of the British East India Company. He fought the Battle of Plassey in 1757 but was 
defeated due to betrayal by his own men. Siraj ud Daula was captured and killed the same year, marking the 
start of British control in Bengal.
Q. Who was Mir Jaffer? [4]
Ans: Mir Jafar was a military commander in Bengal, born in 1691. In his early life, he served under the Nawabs 
of Bengal and gained military experience. He betrayed Nawab Siraj ud Daula in the Battle of Plassey in 1757 
and supported the British. As a reward, the British made him the Nawab of Bengal, but he remained under their 
control. Mir Jafar died in 1765, remembered in history as a symbol of betrayal.
Q. Who was Mir Qasim? [4]
Ans: Mir Qasim was born in 1729 and became the Nawab of Bengal after Mir Jafar. He tried to strengthen 
Bengal by reforming administration and army. He opposed the British trade privileges which led to conflict. He 
fought against the British in the Battle of Buxar (1764). He lost, fled to Delhi, and died in 1777.

Q. Who was Hyder Ali? [4]
Ans: Hyder Ali was a brave ruler of Mysore, born in 1720 in a soldier’s family. In his early life, he joined the 
Mysore army and rose to power due to his courage and skill. He became the ruler of Mysore and modernized 
his army with the help of the French. Hyder Ali fought many battles against the British to protect his state. He 
died in 1782 during the Second Anglo-Mysore War.
Q. Who was Tipu Sultan? [4]
Ans: Tipu Sultan was born in 1751, the son of Hyder Ali, ruler of Mysore. He became the Sultan of Mysore 
after his father’s death. He was famous for his bravery, use of rockets in war, and reforms in administration. He 
strongly resisted the British in the Anglo-Mysore Wars. He was killed in 1799 while defending Seringapatam 
against the British.
7 Mark Questions
Q1. Why Mughal Empire declined after the reign of Aurangzeb? [7]
Ans: After Aurangzeb’s death in 1707, the Mughal throne was inherited by weak and incapable rulers. Unlike 
strong emperors such as Akbar, Jahangir, and Shah Jahan, the later Mughal kings were more interested in 
luxury than in governing. This led to court conspiracies, corruption, and constant struggles for succession 
among princes. The empire, without a strong leader, became unstable and lost control over its vast territories.
The authority of the Mughal throne weakened, and powerful nobles and regional rulers began acting 
independently. This directly contributed to the decline of the Mughal Empire.
During and after Aurangzeb’s reign, several regional powers like the Marathas in the Deccan, Sikhs in Punjab, 
and Rajputs in Rajasthan gained strength. Aurangzeb’s long wars drained the empire’s treasury and weakened 
its army, making it difficult to suppress these powers. After his death, these regional forces expanded and 
established their own rule, challenging Mughal supremacy. The Mughal Empire broke into smaller independent 
states, and the central authority at Delhi was reduced to only symbolic power. This fragmentation was a major 
cause of decline.
The weakness of the Mughal rulers after Aurangzeb invited foreign invaders like Nadir Shah of Persia (1739) 
and Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan. These invasions caused heavy destruction, looting of wealth, and loss 
of life. The invasion of Nadir Shah, for example, drained the empire of immense riches, including the Peacock 
Throne. These invasions destroyed the prestige of the Mughal dynasty and further weakened its economy and 
military. People lost confidence in the Mughals as protectors, which sped up the decline of the empire.
Q2. How Aurangzeb contributed in the decline of Mughal empire? [7]
Ans: Aurangzeb abandoned the policy of religious tolerance followed by earlier emperors like Akbar. He re￾imposed the Jizya tax on non-Muslims and destroyed some temples, which created resentment among Hindus. 
This reduced the loyalty of Rajputs and other Hindu nobles who had previously supported the Mughal Empire.
The loss of cooperation from important Hindu communities weakened the unity of the empire and fueled 
rebellions, directly contributing to the decline.
Aurangzeb spent nearly 25 years fighting wars in the Deccan against the Marathas, Bijapur, and Golconda. 
These wars consumed enormous amounts of money and exhausted the Mughal army. While Aurangzeb was 
busy in the south, the northern provinces became neglected and lawless. The empire’s treasury became empty, 
the army weakened, and regional powers like the Marathas grew stronger, which made the empire unstable and 
led towards decline.

Aurangzeb tried to personally control every aspect of government without trusting his nobles. He dismissed 
capable ministers and generals, relying instead on his own decisions. This made administration less effective, as 
it became impossible for one man to manage such a vast empire. Corruption increased, governance became 
weak, and the empire lost efficiency. This mismanagement created instability, which hastened the decline of the 
Mughal Empire.
Q. How foreign invasions contributed in the decline of Mughal Empire? [7]
Ans: Nadir Shah of Persia invaded India and defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal. He plundered Delhi, 
carried away enormous wealth including the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor diamond, and massacred 
thousands of people. This invasion left the Mughal treasury empty, destroyed Delhi’s prestige, and exposed the 
weakness of the Mughal army. It encouraged other foreign powers to attack India, directly weakening the 
empire.
Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan invaded India several times between 1748 and 1767. He looted Punjab, 
Delhi, and other regions, causing massive destruction. His repeated attacks created lawlessness and made 
people lose faith in the Mughals as protectors. The empire lost control over north-western provinces, its 
economy suffered badly, and regional powers like the Sikhs and Marathas became stronger. This greatly 
weakened Mughal authority.
The foreign invasions weakened the central power so much that regional rulers, like the Marathas and Sikhs, 
declared independence. At the same time, the British East India Company took advantage of this weakness and 
slowly expanded its control over India. The Mughal Empire was reduced to a symbolic authority in Delhi, while 
real power shifted to regional states and the British. This marked the practical end of Mughal power.

Part 2: Arrival & Expansion of British East India Company 
4 Mark Questions
Q1. What was British East India Company? [4]
Ans: The British East India Company was a trading company formed in 1600 by English merchants. Its main 
work was to trade spices, silk, cotton, and tea with India and other Asian countries. Gradually, it built its own 
army, captured territories, and interfered in Indian politics. The Company won important battles like Plassey 
(1757) and Buxar (1764), gaining control over Bengal. Its rule led to corruption and oppression, so in 1858 the 
British Government ended its power and took direct control of India.
Q2. Who was Warren Hasting? [4]
Ans: Warren Hastings was the first Governor-General of Bengal (1773–1785). He introduced reforms in 
revenue collection, justice, and administration. He also strengthened British control through alliances with 
Indian rulers. His policies laid the foundation of British rule in India. He was later accused of corruption but 
acquitted in England.

DIFFICULT TERMS USED IN SECTION 2
1. Separate electorates: 
Separate electorates mean Muslims and Hindus would vote only for their own community’s representatives. Muslims vote 
for Muslims and Hindus vote for Hindus.
2. Joint electorates: 
Joint electorates mean all people, no matter Muslim or Hindu, vote together and choose the same representatives. There is 
no separate voting system for different communities.
3. Legislative Council: 
A Legislative Council is a law-making group in the government. It discusses and passes laws for the country or a 
province.
4. Executive Council: 
An Executive Council is a group of officials who help run the government. They make and carry out decisions and look 
after daily work of administration.
5. Judiciary: 
Judiciary means the court system of a country. It includes judges and courts that give justice and decide cases according to 
law.
6. Bi-Cameral Parliament: 
A bicameral parliament has two houses (two parts) for making laws. Example: Upper House + Lower House.
7. Uni-Cameral Parliament: 
A unicameral parliament has only one house (one part) to make laws. It is simpler and has fewer members.
8. Unitary form of government: 
A unitary government is a system where all powers are controlled by the central (national) government. Provinces or local 
governments only get powers that the central government gives them.
9. Federal form of government: 
A federal government is a system where power is divided between the central government and provincial/state 
governments. Both have their own powers which are written in the constitution.
