Another reason was that the partition increased hatred between Hindus and Muslims instead of helping in 
administration. The British realized that the division had created deep political and communal problems. The 
two communities started blaming each other, which made governance harder. To reduce communal conflict, 
they decided to reunite Bengal. This shows that the British reversed the decision to avoid more division in 
Indian society.
Another major reason was the rise of the Swadeshi Movement, which started as a reaction to the partition. 
People began boycotting British goods and promoting Indian-made products to show their protest. The 
movement hurt the British economy and spread the spirit of nationalism across India. This economic and 
political pressure made the British realize their policy had failed. It shows that the Swadeshi Movement played 
a key role in forcing the British to reverse the partition.
Q5. Why Simla deputation was so important for the Muslims in India? [7]
Ans: The Simla Deputation was important for Muslims because it gave them their first opportunity to directly 
present their political concerns to the British government. The deputation demanded separate electorates so 
Muslims could elect their own representatives. This step showed Muslims’ growing political awareness and 
unity. As a result, the British started recognizing Muslims as a separate political community. This clearly shows 
why the Simla Deputation was a turning point in Muslim political identity in India.
The Simla Deputation was also significant because it inspired Muslims to form their own political party. After 
seeing the power of united representation, Muslim leaders established the All India Muslim League in 
December 1906. This gave Muslims a proper political platform to protect their rights and interests in future 
politics. The League later became the main voice of Muslims in India. Therefore, the Simla Deputation directly 
led to the political awakening of Muslims.
Another reason the Simla Deputation was so important is that it gained British support for Muslim demands. 
The British accepted the idea of separate electorates and promised fair representation for Muslims in future 
councils. This victory gave Muslims confidence that their unity could bring real results. It also improved their 
relations with the British, which benefited them in early political reforms. Hence, the Simla Deputation 
strengthened Muslims’ position in Indian politics.

Q6. Why was Muslim League formed in 1906? [7]
Ans: The Muslim League was formed in 1906 because the Indian National Congress was seen as a Hindu￾dominated party. Congress mostly focused on Hindu interests and ignored Muslim concerns in its demands. 
Many Muslim leaders feared that Hindus would dominate all political power if the British left India. This 
created a sense of insecurity among Muslims. Therefore, Muslims formed their own party to protect their 
political and religious rights.
The rise of the Arya Samaj movement also played an important role in the formation of the Muslim League. 
Arya Samaj promoted Hindu nationalism and started the Shuddhi Movement to convert Muslims back to 
Hinduism. This created tension and fear among Muslims about their religious and cultural identity. They felt the 
need for an organization that could defend their community. Hence, the Muslim League was formed to 
safeguard Muslim beliefs and unity against such movements.
The success of the Simla Deputation in 1906 encouraged Muslims to organize politically. Muslim leaders 
realized that unity and peaceful representation could help them achieve their goals. The British accepted their 
demand for separate electorates, which gave Muslims confidence in their political strength. This success 
motivated them to form a permanent political body. Therefore, the Muslim League was established to continue 
representing Muslim interests effectively in Indian politics.
Q7. Why were Morley Minto reforms introduced by the British in India? [7]
Ans: The Morley-Minto Reforms were introduced because the British wanted to calm down the growing 
political unrest in India. After the Partition of Bengal in 1905, both Hindus and Muslims started demanding 
more political rights. The British feared these protests could turn violent. So, they introduced the reforms in 
1909 to give Indians a small share in government and reduce anger against British rule. This shows that the 
reforms were meant to maintain peace and control in India.
Another reason for introducing the Morley-Minto Reforms was to reward loyal communities, especially 
Muslims. After the Simla Deputation of 1906, the British realized Muslims were loyal and cooperative. 
Therefore, they introduced separate electorates to please Muslims and win their political support. This helped 
the British balance power between Hindus and Muslims. Hence, the reforms were used to strengthen British 
influence through the policy of “divide and rule.”
The British also introduced these reforms to give Indians limited experience in administration. They allowed 
some Indians to become members of Legislative Councils, though their powers were very small. This was 
meant to show that the British were promoting political progress and modernization. It helped the British 
improve their image after years of criticism. Thus, the reforms were introduced to give an appearance of 
political reform while keeping real power in British hands.
Q8. Why were Morley Minto reforms opposed by the Indian National Congress? [7]
Ans: The Indian National Congress opposed the Morley-Minto Reforms because they gave very limited powers 
to Indians. Although Indians were allowed to join the Legislative Councils, they had no real authority to make 
or change laws. Most decisions were still controlled by the British officials. Congress felt that these reforms 
were only a show and did not bring true self-government. This is why Congress rejected them as meaningless 
and unfair.

Another reason for opposition was the introduction of separate electorates for Muslims. Congress believed this
step would divide Indians on religious lines and weaken their unity against British rule. They argued that the 
British were using the policy of “divide and rule” to keep Hindus and Muslims apart. This division made it 
harder to form a united movement for independence. Hence, Congress strongly opposed the communal feature 
of the reforms.
The Indian National Congress wanted larger councils so more Indians could join governance, but the British 
only made limited changes. They had no plan to give real power or introduce democracy in India. Their aim 
was to create an appearance of reform while keeping full control. John Morley’s attitude showed their rejection 
of true political freedom. Therefore, Congress opposed the Morley-Minto Reforms for ignoring genuine Indian 
demands. 
Q9. Why Lucknow Pact was signed in 1916? [7]
Ans: The Lucknow Pact was signed in 1916 because both the Muslim League and the Indian National Congress 
wanted to unite against British rule. They realized that their separate efforts were not strong enough to gain 
political rights. By joining hands, they could put more pressure on the British for reforms. This unity created 
hope for self-government in India. Therefore, the pact was signed to strengthen the national struggle through 
Hindu-Muslim cooperation.
Another reason for the Lucknow Pact was the change in leadership of the Muslim League. When leaders like 
Jinnah joined both the League and Congress, they encouraged cooperation between the two parties. They 
believed unity would benefit both Muslims and Hindus in achieving common political goals. This helped reduce 
mistrust between the communities for some time. Hence, the pact was signed to promote joint efforts for India’s 
political progress.
The Lucknow Pact was also signed because both parties wanted to take advantage of Britain’s weakness during 
World War I. The British were busy in the war and could not easily ignore Indian demands. Congress and the 
League used this opportunity to demand greater participation in government. Their unity made their demands 
stronger and more difficult for the British to reject. Therefore, the pact was signed to gain political benefits 
during a time of British difficulty.
Q10. Why were Montague Chelmsford reforms introduced by the British in India? [7]
Ans: The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms were introduced because the British wanted to calm down the 
growing demand for self-government in India. After World War I, Indians expected political rewards for their 
support during the war. The British feared more protests and unrest if they ignored these demands. So, they 
promised gradual participation of Indians in governance. Therefore, the reforms were introduced to reduce 
political pressure and maintain British control peacefully.
Another reason for introducing the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms was to show that Britain believed in the 
principle of “responsible government.” The British government wanted to prove to the world that it was modern 
and fair, especially after the war. By giving Indians limited powers in provinces, they tried to show progress 
toward self-rule. However, real authority still remained with the British officials. Thus, the reforms were 
introduced to improve Britain’s image while keeping control in their hands.

The reforms were also introduced to divide responsibility between British rulers and Indian politicians. Through 
a system called dyarchy, some subjects like education and health were given to Indian ministers, while 
important areas like defense remained under British control. This made Indians feel involved but still dependent 
on the British. The system was meant to train Indians for future administration. Therefore, the reforms were 
introduced to create controlled participation without losing British authority.
Q11. Why Montague Chelmsford received a lot of criticism from the Indians? [7]
Ans: The Montague-Chelmsford Reforms were criticized because they gave very limited powers to Indians. 
Although Indians were included in provincial governments, all major decisions were still controlled by the 
British governors. The British officials could overrule Indian ministers anytime. This made Indians feel that the 
reforms were only a show, not real power-sharing. Therefore, people criticized the reforms for failing to give 
true self-government.
Another reason for criticism was the unfair system of dyarchy. Under this system, subjects were divided into 
“transferred” and “reserved” categories, where Indians handled minor departments like education, while the 
British kept control over important ones like finance and police. This made Indians feel humiliated and 
powerless. Instead of creating equality, it increased dissatisfaction. Hence, the reforms were opposed for 
treating Indians as untrustworthy in key matters.
The reforms were also criticized because they did not meet the expectations raised during World War I. Indians 
had supported the British in the war, hoping for greater political freedom in return. But when the reforms came, 
they were slow, limited, and disappointing. Many leaders felt betrayed by British promises of self-rule. 
Therefore, the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms faced strong criticism for failing to fulfill Indian hopes and 
demands.

CHATPER 7: KHILAFAT MOVEMENT 1919 - 1924
4 Mark Questions
Q1. What was Khilafat Movement? [4]
Ans: The Khilafat Movement started in 1919 to protect the position of the Turkish Caliph, who was the spiritual 
leader of Muslims worldwide. After World War I, the British and their allies broke up the Ottoman Empire, 
which deeply hurt Muslim feelings. Indian Muslim leaders like Maulana Muhammad Ali and Maulana Shaukat 
Ali began a movement to defend the Caliph’s authority. Hindus, led by Gandhi, also supported it to unite 
Indians against British rule. Although the movement failed when the Caliphate ended in 1924, it awakened 
strong political unity among Indian Muslims.
Q2. Describe the Khilafat Conferences. [4]
Ans: The Khilafat Conferences were held between 1919 and 1924 to protect the Turkish Caliphate and show 
Muslim unity in India. The first major conference was held in Delhi in 1919, followed by others in Calcutta, 
Karachi, and Lucknow. Muslim leaders like Maulana Muhammad Ali, Shaukat Ali, and Maulana Azad led 
these meetings to protest against British actions after World War I. They passed resolutions urging the British to 
respect the Caliph’s position and Muslim rights. Although the movement later failed, the conferences united 
Muslims politically and strengthened their struggle for independence.
Q3. What was Moplah’s uprising? [4]
Ans: The Moplah Uprising took place in Malabar, Kerala, in 1921 during the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation 
Movements. The Moplah Muslims, who were poor farmers, rose against British officials and local Hindu 
landlords who supported the British. The revolt began as a protest against oppression but turned violent. The 
British used heavy force to crush the rebellion, killing and arresting thousands. Though it failed, it showed the 
deep anger of Muslims against British rule.
Q4. What was Wagon Tragedy? [4]
Ans: The Wagon Tragedy occurred in 1921 after the Moplah Uprising in Kerala. The British arrested hundreds 
of Moplah rebels and packed them tightly into closed railway wagons to be sent to prison. Due to suffocation 
and lack of air, around 70 prisoners died during the journey. This brutal act exposed British cruelty towards 
Indians. The tragedy increased anger and sympathy for the freedom fighters across India.
Q5. What was Chauri Chaura incident? [4]
Ans: The Chauri Chaura Incident happened in 1922 in a village near Gorakhpur, Uttar Pradesh. During the 
Non-Cooperation Movement, angry protesters set fire to a police station, killing 22 policemen. Mahatma 
Gandhi was shocked by the violence and immediately called off the movement. The incident showed how 
quickly peaceful protests could turn violent. It also weakened the momentum of the freedom struggle for some 
time.
Q6. What was Hijrat Movement? [4]
Ans: The Hijrat Movement started in 1920 when Indian Muslims decided to migrate from India to Afghanistan. 
It began after the failure of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movements, when Muslims believed India was 
no longer safe for Islam under British rule. Thousands of Muslims sold their belongings and left for 
Afghanistan, hoping to live under an Islamic government. However, the Afghan government refused to accept

them, and many suffered or died on the way. The movement failed, but it showed the deep faith and sacrifice of 
Indian Muslims.
Q7. What was Treaty of Versailles? [4]
Ans: The Treaty of Versailles was signed in 1919 between the Allied Powers and Germany after World War I. 
Germany was blamed for the war and forced to pay heavy reparations and lose its colonies. The treaty also 
reduced Germany’s army and territory. It created the League of Nations to maintain world peace. However, its 
harsh terms caused resentment in Germany and later led to the rise of Hitler and World War II.
Q8. What was Treaty of Sèvres? [4]
Ans: The Treaty of Sèvres was signed in 1920 between the Allied Powers and the Ottoman Empire after World 
War I. It broke up the Ottoman Empire and took away large parts of its territory, giving land to Greece, Britain, 
and France. The Caliph’s power was reduced, and Turkey lost control over Arab lands. This deeply hurt 
Muslims around the world, including those in India. The harsh terms of this treaty led to great anger and 
became a main cause of the Khilafat Movement.
Q9. What was Treaty of Lausanne? [4]
Ans: The Treaty of Lausanne was signed in 1923 between the Allied Powers and Turkey, led by Mustafa Kemal 
Atatürk. It replaced the harsh Treaty of Sèvres and recognized Turkey as an independent republic. Turkey 
regained control over its lost territories and foreign influence was reduced. This treaty ended the occupation of 
Turkey by foreign powers. It marked the success of Turkish nationalists and ended the Khilafat Movement in 
India.
Q9. Who was Sultan Mehmed VI? [4]
Ans: Sultan Mehmed VI was the last ruler of the Ottoman Empire, who came to power in 1918 after World War 
I. He faced a very difficult time as the Ottoman Empire had lost the war and was being divided by the Allied 
powers. He tried to save his empire by cooperating with the British but failed to protect it. During his rule, 
Mustafa Kemal Atatürk started the Turkish National Movement against foreign control. Finally, in 1922, the 
Sultanate was abolished, and Mehmed VI was sent into exile, ending the Ottoman rule of over 600 years..
Q10. Who was Mustafa Kemal Atatürk Pasha? [4]
Ans: Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was a Turkish army officer and leader who fought against foreign powers after 
World War I. He led the Turkish War of Independence and defeated the forces that tried to divide Turkey. After 
victory, he ended the Ottoman Sultanate in 1922 and later the Caliphate in 1924. He became the first President 
of modern Turkey and introduced many reforms to modernize the country. Atatürk changed Turkey into a 
modern, secular, and democratic state, earning the title “Father of the Turks.
Q11. Who were Ali Brothers? [4]
Ans: The Ali Brothers were Maulana Mohammad Ali and Maulana Shaukat Ali, famous Muslim leaders from 
India. They started their political work to support the Khilafat Movement after World War I. They wanted to 
protect the Ottoman Caliph and also fight for India’s independence from British rule. The brothers worked 
closely with Gandhi during the Non-Cooperation Movement. Their efforts united Muslims and Hindus for a 
time, but the movement failed when the Caliphate was abolished in 1924.

the war, the British had promised that no harm would be done to the Turkish Empire if Muslims supported

against British injustice.
The Khilafat Movement also emerged because Indian Muslims wanted to unite politically and religiously. 
Leaders like the Ali Brothers, Maulana Azad, and Gandhi urged Muslims to come together to defend the Caliph 
and their rights in India. The movement became a symbol of Muslim unity and political awakening. It also 
joined hands with the Non-Cooperation Movement led by Gandhi. Therefore, the Khilafat Movement was 
launched to unite Muslims and resist British control.
Q2. Why Gandhi joined the Khilafat Movement? [7]
Ans: Gandhi joined the Khilafat Movement because he saw it as a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims against 
British rule. He believed that cooperation between the two major communities would make the struggle for 
independence stronger. The Khilafat cause gave him an opportunity to bring both groups on one platform. 
Gandhi thought this unity would help end British control peacefully. Therefore, he supported the movement to 
strengthen national unity and the freedom struggle.
Another reason Gandhi joined the Khilafat Movement was his belief in non-violence and moral protest. The 
Muslim leaders were promoting peaceful resistance against British injustice, which matched Gandhi’s own 
philosophy of Satyagraha. He saw the movement as a peaceful way to express anger over British betrayal after 
World War I. This encouraged him to work closely with Muslim leaders. Hence, Gandhi supported the Khilafat 
Movement because it followed his principle of non-violent protest.
Gandhi also joined the Khilafat Movement to gain wider support for the Indian National Congress. By 
supporting Muslim demands, he hoped Muslims would also back the Congress in its fight for independence. 
This cooperation increased Congress’s popularity across India. It also made the anti-British movement stronger 
than before. Therefore, Gandhi joined the Khilafat Movement to combine both religious and political struggles 
against British rule.
Q3. Why Khilafat Movement failed? [7]
Ans: The Khilafat Movement failed mainly because of the Chauri Chaura incident in 1922. During this event, 
angry protesters killed several policemen by burning a police station in Uttar Pradesh. Gandhi, who believed in 
non-violence, was deeply shocked and immediately ended the Non-Cooperation Movement, which was linked 
with Khilafat. This sudden end weakened the spirit of the movement. Therefore, the Chauri Chaura incident 
became a major reason for the failure of the Khilafat Movement.

Another reason for the failure of the Khilafat Movement was the Moplah Uprising in 1921. The Moplah 
Muslims of Kerala started a violent rebellion against the British and Hindu landlords. The movement, which 
was supposed to be peaceful, turned into violent clashes and loss of lives. This created mistrust between Hindus 
and Muslims, breaking the unity Gandhi had built. Hence, the Moplah Uprising weakened the movement and 
pushed it towards failure.
The Hijrat Movement also caused the Khilafat Movement to fail. Many Muslims, thinking India was no longer 
safe for Islam, migrated to Afghanistan in protest against British rule. However, they faced great hardships as 
Afghanistan refused to accept them, and most had to return in misery. This caused disappointment and loss of 
faith in the movement’s leaders. Therefore, the failure of the Hijrat Movement led to the overall collapse of the 
Khilafat Movement.
Q4. Why Hijrat Movement failed? [7]
Ans: The Hijrat Movement failed because Muslims who migrated to Afghanistan were not welcomed by the 
Afghan government. They had expected to find refuge in an Islamic country, but Afghanistan was already 
facing its own economic and political problems. As a result, thousands of Indian Muslims were forced to return 
home. Many lost their savings and property during the journey. Therefore, the lack of support from Afghanistan 
led to the failure of the Hijrat Movement.
Another reason for the failure of the Hijrat Movement was poor planning and lack of organization. The 
movement began emotionally without proper arrangements for food, shelter, or safety for the migrants. Most 
people sold everything they had before leaving India and suffered greatly on the way. Many died due to hunger, 
diseases, and harsh weather. Hence, the unplanned and unprepared migration turned the movement into a 
tragedy and caused its failure.
The Hijrat Movement also failed because it was based on false hopes and wrong beliefs. The leaders had told 
people that leaving British India was a religious duty and Afghanistan would offer them a better Islamic life. 
But when those promises were not fulfilled, Muslims lost trust in the movement and its leaders. Their return to 
India in misery caused deep disappointment. Therefore, the false expectations and broken promises led to the 
failure of the Hijrat Movement.

4 Mark Questions
Q1. What were Delhi Proposals? [4]
Ans: The Delhi Proposals were presented by the Muslim League in 1927 to protect Muslim political rights. 
Muslims agreed to give up separate electorates if their demands were accepted. They demanded one-third 
representation in the central legislature, separate status for Sindh, and reforms in Balochistan and NWFP. These 
proposals aimed to create Hindu-Muslim unity before the Simon Commission’s arrival. However, the Congress 
rejected them, increasing political tension between both communities.
Q2. What was Simon Commission? [4]
Ans: The Simon Commission was sent by the British government in 1927 to suggest political reforms for India. 
He recommended federal form of government in India, diarchy was abolished, rejected the demand of Muslim 
for the one-third seats in the legislative council. It had no Indian members, which angered both the Congress 
and the Muslim League. Indians protested with slogans like “Simon Go Back!”. However, some Muslim 
leaders, including Muhammad Shafi, supported it. The commission later suggested more provincial autonomy, 
but its rejection by Indians increased their demand for self-rule.
Q3. What was Nehru Report? [4]
Ans: INC was not satisfied with Simon Commission and wanted to present its own draft for the future 
constitution of India. The Nehru Report was prepared in 1928 by Motilal Nehru and other Congress leaders in 
reply to the Simon Commission. It suggested dominion status for India, a parliamentary system, and joint 
electorates with no separate representation for Muslims. Muslims opposed it because their political safeguards 
were ignored. This rejection created a deep divide between Hindus and Muslims. It later led Jinnah to present 
his Fourteen Points.
Q4. What were Jinnah’s 14 points? [4]
Ans: Nehru Report was not satisfactory for the Muslims of India, as a reply of its Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad 
Ali Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points in 1929 to safeguard Muslim interests. He demanded separate 
electorates, one-third Muslim representation in the central legislature, and provincial autonomy. He also wanted 
protection of Muslim culture, religion, and language. These points were a clear reply to the Nehru Report. They 
later became the foundation for the Pakistan Movement.
Q4. What was Salt March? [4]
Ans: The Salt March was launched by Mahatma Gandhi in 1930 against the British tax on salt. Gandhi and his 
followers walked from Sabarmati to Dandi, covering 240 miles, to make salt from seawater as an act of protest. 
This movement became a symbol of civil disobedience across India. Thousands of people joined and were 
arrested by the British. Although the tax was not removed, the march united Indians and strengthened the 
freedom struggle.

Q5. What was Allahabad Address? [4]
Ans: The Allahabad Address was delivered by Allama Iqbal in 1930 at the annual session of the Muslim 
League. He proposed the idea of a separate homeland for Muslims in the northwestern areas of India, including 
Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and NWFP. Iqbal believed Muslims were a separate nation with their own religion 
and culture. His speech gave new direction to Muslim politics in India. It later became the foundation for the 
demand for Pakistan.
Q6. What was Gandhi Irwin Pact? [4]
Ans: The Gandhi-Irwin Pact was signed in 1931 between Mahatma Gandhi and Viceroy Lord Irwin. It was 
made to end the Civil Disobedience Movement and prepare for the Second Round Table Conference. The 
British agreed to release political prisoners and allow peaceful protests. In return, Gandhi ended the Civil 
Disobedience Movement. However, no major political gain was achieved, and the pact failed to meet Indian 
expectations.
Q7. What was Communal Award? [4]
Ans: The Communal Award was announced in 1932 by British Prime Minister Ramsay MacDonald. It gave 
separate electorates to different communities like Muslims, Sikhs, and Dalits (Depressed Classes). The decision 
aimed to protect minority rights but divided Indian society further. Many leaders, including Gandhi, opposed it 
because it encouraged separation. The award was later modified after the Poona Pact agreement.
Q8. What was Poona Pact? [4]
Ans: The Poona Pact was signed in 1932 between Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. It was made after 
Gandhi’s protest against separate electorates for the Depressed Classes under the Communal Award. Both 
leaders agreed to reserve seats for Dalits in legislatures instead of giving them separate electorates. This pact 
ended Gandhi’s fast and brought peace for some time. However, it did not end caste discrimination completely 
in India.
Q9. What was Government Act of India 1935? [4]
Ans: The Government of India Act of 1935 was the longest act passed by the British Parliament for India. It 
introduced provincial autonomy, giving provinces the right to form their own governments. It also proposed the 
creation of an All-India Federation and continued separate electorates for minorities. The act gave more 
political power to Indians but the British still controlled defense and foreign affairs. It became the base for 
India’s future constitution.
Q9. Describe the elections of 1936-37 in India? [4]
Ans: The elections of 1936–37 was held under the Government of India Act 1935 and were the first provincial 
elections in India. Out of 11 provinces, the Congress won in 8 provinces, securing about 716 out of 1,585 seats, 
mostly in Hindu-majority areas like U.P., Bihar, and Central Provinces. The Muslim League, on the other hand, 
won only about 109 out of 482 Muslim seats, performing well only in Bengal and Punjab. Congress refused to 
share power with the League in provinces where Muslims lived in large numbers. This deepened mistrust and 
widened the political gap between Hindus and Muslims in India.

Q10. What was Wardha Scheme? [4]
Ans: The Wardha Scheme was introduced in 1937 by Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress. It 
aimed to make basic education in India based on handicrafts and manual work so students could earn while 
learning. The scheme was meant to promote self-reliance and remove dependence on British-style education. 
Moreover, bow down in front of Gandhi’s portray was compulsory. However, it focused mainly on Hindu 
values and ignored Islamic education. This created fear among Muslims and led to opposition from the Muslim 
League.
Q11. What was Vidya Mandir Scheme? [4]
Ans: The Vidya Mandir Scheme was introduced by the Congress government in some provinces after the 1937 
elections. It aimed to spread Hindu culture and language (especially Hindi) in schools under the name of 
“national education.” Many schools began promoting Hindu prayers and songs. Muslims felt this scheme tried 
to weaken their culture and religion. As a result, it increased Muslim opposition to Congress rule and 
strengthened support for the Muslim League.
Q12. What was Wande Mataram Song? [4]
Ans: The “Wande Mataram” song was written by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee in the 1870s and later included in 
his novel Anandamath. It praised Mother India and became a national song for the Indian National Congress. 
However, its words and ideas were based on Hindu goddess worship, which hurt Muslim feelings. Muslims 
refused to sing it in schools and political meetings. This issue increased religious division between Hindus and 
Muslims in Indian politics.
Q13. What was Day of deliverance? [4]
Ans: The Day of Deliverance was observed on 22nd December 1939 by Muslims in India, led by Quaid-e￾Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. It was celebrated after the Congress ministries resigned from all provinces when 
Britain declared India’s participation in World War II without consulting Indian leaders. Jinnah declared this 
day as a mark of relief from Congress’s oppressive rule during 1937–39. Muslims held meetings and thanked 
Allah for their freedom from Congress domination. The event strengthened the Muslim League’s position as the 
true representative of Indian Muslims.

7 Mark Questions
Q1. Why Muslim league presented Delhi Proposals in 1927? [7]
Ans: The Muslim League presented the Delhi Proposals in 1927 to show its willingness to cooperate with the 
Indian National Congress for constitutional reforms. Muslim leaders wanted to prove that they were ready to 
work together for India’s self-government. They hoped this cooperation would strengthen the demand for 
political rights from the British. It was also an effort to bring unity between Hindus and Muslims. Therefore, the 
proposals were presented to promote political harmony and national progress.
Another reason was fear of majority domination as Congress grew stronger, so Muslim leaders wanted firm 
safeguards. They asked for separate electorates, reserved seats and weightage in provincial assemblies to protect 
Muslim political rights. By presenting the Delhi Proposals they aimed to fix these protections before any new 
constitution was made. This showed the League wanted security for Muslims within future government 
structures. Therefore, the proposals were presented to ensure Muslim interests would not be sidelined.
The Delhi Proposals were also presented to replace the 1916 Lucknow Pact with a new agreement suitable for 
changing political conditions. Since many Congress leaders had started opposing separate electorates, Muslims 
felt the need for a new understanding. By offering fresh terms, they tried to keep political dialogue open 
between both communities. This showed the League’s flexibility and maturity in politics. Therefore, the Delhi 
Proposals were presented to renew cooperation and ensure Muslim participation in India’s future constitution.
Q2. Why Simon Commission came to India? [7]
Ans: The Simon Commission came to India in 1928 to review how the Montague-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 
were working. The British government wanted to study whether Indians were ready for more political power 
and self-government. The commission was supposed to suggest changes for better administration. It was a step 
to plan the next constitutional reforms for India. Therefore, the British sent the Simon Commission to examine 
the political progress of the country.
Another reason for sending the Simon Commission was the growing demand for independence in India. Many 
protests and movements were taking place against British rule. The British government wanted to calm the 
situation by showing that it cared about India’s political future. By sending the commission, they hoped to 
reduce public anger and delay the demand for full freedom. Hence, the Simon Commission was sent to control 
rising political pressure in India.
The Simon Commission was also sent because the British wanted to keep full control over the reform process. 
They did not trust Indian leaders to make constitutional changes themselves. By forming a commission with 
only British members, they ensured that the decisions would favor their interests. This showed that Britain 
wanted to appear helpful while still maintaining authority. Therefore, the Simon Commission came to India to 
secure British dominance through controlled reforms.

Q3. Why Simon Commission was so unpopular among the Indians / rejected by the Indians? [7]
Ans: The Simon Commission was unpopular because it had no Indian members. All seven members of the 
commission were British, which deeply offended the Indian people. They believed that Indians were capable of 
discussing their own political future. The exclusion showed that the British did not trust Indian leaders. 
Therefore, Indians rejected the Simon Commission for ignoring their representation and self-respect.
Another reason for its unpopularity was that it came at a time when Indians were demanding self-rule. The 
British had promised more participation after World War I, but the commission gave no sign of real 
independence. Instead, it showed that the British wanted to continue ruling India. This angered both the 
Congress and the Muslim League. Hence, the Simon Commission was opposed because its betrayed India’s 
hopes for freedom.
The Simon Commission was also unpopular because Indians were not consulted before it was sent. The British 
made all the decisions in London without asking Indian leaders about their opinions or needs. This made people 
feel insulted and ignored in matters that directly affected their country. Indians wanted to be part of decisions 
about their own future. Therefore, the Simon Commission was strongly opposed because it disrespected Indian 
opinion and political rights.
Q4. Why Nehru Report so disappointing for the Muslims of India? [7]
Ans: The Nehru Report was disappointing for Muslims because it rejected the idea of separate electorates. 
Muslims believed separate electorates protected their political rights and gave them fair representation. 
However, the report demanded joint electorates, which meant Muslims could be outvoted by the Hindu 
majority. This created fear of losing their voice in politics. Therefore, Muslims were unhappy as the report 
ignored one of their main political safeguards.
Another reason the Nehru Report disappointed Muslims was the rejection of their demand for one-third 
representation in the central legislature. Muslims wanted this share to ensure they had a strong voice in national 
decisions, even though they were a minority. The report, however, gave them far fewer seats, reducing their 
political influence. This was seen as unfair and against Muslim interests. Hence, the report was opposed 
because it denied Muslims proper representation in the government.
The Nehru Report also disappointed Muslims because it rejected the idea of a federal form of government. 
Muslims supported federalism since it gave more powers to provinces where they were in majority, like Punjab 
and Bengal. The report instead proposed a strong central government, which meant Hindu-majority provinces 
would dominate. This made Muslims fear losing control over their own regions. Therefore, Muslims opposed 
the Nehru Report as it ignored their demand for a fair federal system.
Q4. Why Mohammad Ali Jinnah presented his 14 points? [7]
Ans: Jinnah presented his Fourteen Points because the Nehru Report had rejected the idea of separate 
electorates for Muslims. He believed separate electorates were necessary to protect Muslim political rights and 
ensure fair representation. Without them, Muslims could easily be overpowered by the Hindu majority in 
elections. Jinnah wanted to restore this safeguard for his community’s protection. Therefore, he included 
separate electorates in his Fourteen Points to defend Muslim political identity.

Jinnah also presented the Fourteen Points because the Nehru Report denied Muslims one-third representation in 
the central legislature. Muslims demanded this share so they could have a strong voice in national matters 
despite being fewer in number. By giving them much less, the report weakened Muslim influence in politics. 
Jinnah saw this as unfair treatment of Muslims. Hence, he included the one-third representation demand in his 
Fourteen Points to secure equal political power for Muslims.
Another reason Jinnah presented the Fourteen Points was the rejection of the federal system in the Nehru 
Report. Muslims supported federalism because it gave more authority to provinces where they were in majority, 
such as Punjab and Bengal. The report’s plan for a strong central government meant Hindus would dominate 
national politics. Jinnah wanted to prevent this imbalance of power. Therefore, he included the demand for a 
federal form of government in his Fourteen Points to protect Muslim-majority provinces.
Q5. Why Allahabad Address was so important for the Muslims of India? [7]
Ans: The Allahabad Address was important because Allama Iqbal clearly presented the idea of a separate 
homeland for Muslims. He said that Muslims were a separate nation with their own religion, culture, and way of 
life. He suggested that Muslim-majority areas like Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan, and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa should 
be combined into one state. This gave Muslims a clear political goal for the future. Therefore, the address 
became the foundation of the demand for Pakistan.
Another reason for its importance was that Iqbal gave new hope and direction to the Muslims of India. At that 
time, Muslims were politically weak and confused after the failure of the Khilafat and Non-Cooperation 
movements. Iqbal’s speech reminded them of their separate identity and inspired them to struggle for their 
rights. His vision united Muslims under one cause. Hence, the Allahabad Address was important because it 
revived Muslim confidence and political awakening.
The Allahabad Address was also important because it guided future Muslim leaders like Quaid-e-Azam 
Muhammad Ali Jinnah. Iqbal’s idea of a separate Muslim state later became the base of Jinnah’s Two-Nation 
Theory and the Pakistan Movement. It gave a clear direction to Muslim League policies in the coming years. 
The dream shown by Iqbal in 1930 became a reality in 1947. Therefore, the address was a turning point in 
Muslim political history.
Q6. Why Round Table conferences were conducted during 1930 - 1932? [7]
Ans: The Round Table Conferences were held because the Simon Commission of 1927 did not include any 
Indians, which made Indians angry. Indians wanted their views to be heard in making new laws. The British 
understood that they needed Indian leaders’ support for future plans to work. So, they arranged meetings to 
discuss India’s political future with them. This showed that the British had to involve Indians after the Simon 
Commission failed.
Another reason for the Round Table Conferences was that Indians were demanding self-government. The Civil 
Disobedience Movement and other protests showed they would not accept British rule without change. The 
British wanted to reduce tension and bring peace. So, they arranged meetings to discuss a new political system. 
These conferences were meant to calm the situation and talk about giving India more freedom.
The Round Table Conferences were also held to settle disputes between different communities in India. Hindus, 
Muslims, and other groups disagreed over political rights and representation. The British wanted all 
communities to work together on a common plan. Leaders like Jinnah and Gandhi were invited to share their 
opinions. These conferences aimed to create unity and make a political plan that included everyone.

Q7. Why Round Table conferences during 1930 – 1932 couldn’t achieve success? [7]
Ans: The Round Table Conferences failed because the Congress Party did not attend the First Conference in 
1930. Since the Congress was the largest political party in India, its absence made the discussions one-sided and 
incomplete. Without Congress participation, no major decisions could represent all Indians. This weakened the 
conference from the start. Therefore, the absence of Congress was a major reason why the Round Table 
Conferences could not achieve success.
Another reason for the failure was the lack of unity among Indian political groups. The Muslim League, Hindu 
Mahasabha, Sikhs, and other minorities all had different demands and could not agree on key constitutional 
issues. This disagreement made it impossible to present a single Indian viewpoint. The British took advantage 
of these divisions and delayed reforms. Hence, internal disunity among Indian leaders led to the failure of the 
Round Table Conferences.
The conferences also failed because the British government was not serious about giving real power to Indians. 
Instead of accepting Indian demands for self-rule, they continued to control major areas like defense and 
finance. Even Gandhi’s efforts in the Second Conference could not change their attitude. The British only 
wanted limited reforms to maintain control over India. Therefore, the Round Table Conferences failed as the 
British were unwilling to share genuine political power.
Q8. Why was the Government Act of India 1935 so important for the Indians? [7]
Ans: The Government of India Act 1935 was important because it introduced provincial autonomy. For the first 
time, Indian ministers were allowed to form governments and make decisions in their own provinces. This gave 
Indians practical experience in running administration and politics. Leaders like Congress and Muslim League 
members took part in elections under this system. Therefore, the Act was important as it increased Indian 
participation in government.
Another reason for its importance was that the Act introduced a federal system. It planned to unite the provinces 
and princely states under one central government. Although the federal part was never fully applied, it showed a 
step toward forming a united Indian constitution. This idea later influenced the political structure of both India 
and Pakistan. Hence, the Act was significant because it laid the foundation for a federal government system.
The Government of India Act 1935 was also important because it expanded voting rights. The number of Indian 
voters increased to about 35 million, allowing more people to take part in elections. This gave Indians a greater 
sense of responsibility and involvement in politics. It helped prepare them for full democratic rule in the future. 
Therefore, the Act played a key role in developing political awareness among the Indian people.
Q9. Why did Indians reject the Government Act 1935? [7]
Ans: Indians rejected the Government of India Act 1935 because the governors still had too much power. Even 
though provincial governments were formed, the British governors could dismiss ministers and reject laws 
anytime. This meant Indian leaders had no real authority in their own provinces. The system looked democratic 
but was still controlled by the British. Therefore, the Act was rejected as it failed to give Indians true political 
control.
Another reason for rejection was that major powers remained in the hands of the British government. Important 
areas like defense, finance, and foreign affairs were not given to Indian ministers. The British used these powers 
to interfere in every major decision. Indians realized that the Act was only a way to continue British dominance. 
Hence, they rejected it because it did not bring real independence or self-rule.

The Act was also opposed because only a few rich people could vote due to strict property qualifications. Most 
ordinary Indians were too poor to meet these conditions, so they were excluded from the elections. This made 
the government unrepresentative and unfair. The people wanted equal voting rights for all adults, not just the 
wealthy. Therefore, Indians rejected the Act as it failed to provide true democracy and equality.
Q10. Why All India Muslim league couldn’t perform well in 1937 elections? [7]
Ans: The All India Muslim League could not perform well in the 1937 elections because it was still weakly 
organized at that time. The League had limited membership, fewer offices, and lacked strong leadership in 
many provinces. Most Muslims were not aware of its aims and did not actively support it. On the other hand, 
the Congress was well-organized and popular among the people. Therefore, the League failed to win many seats 
due to its weak organization and limited influence.
Another reason for the League’s poor performance was that the Congress dominated provincial politics. 
Congress had more resources, better election campaigns, and strong local leaders who influenced the voters. 
Many Muslims also voted for Congress candidates, believing they would protect their interests. This made it 
difficult for the Muslim League to compete effectively. Hence, the League performed poorly as Congress 
controlled most of the provincial assemblies.
The Muslim League also failed because it did not focus on the problems of ordinary Muslims. Its message was

Indian leaders. The Viceroy declared India’s participation in the war against Germany on his own. Congress felt 
disrespected since they were not consulted on such an important matter. This proved that the British still held 
real control over India. So, Congress quit in protest against this unfair and undemocratic decision.

World War II started, Congress asked the British to promise self-rule (Swaraj) in return for India’s help. But the 
British refused to give any such promise. This made Congress realize that the British didn’t plan to end their

they wanted to create problems for the British during the war. They believed this would force the British to talk 
and offer more political rights. It was also a way to show unity and strength among Indian leaders. So, Congress 
resigned in 1939 as a strategy to push for independence.

4 Mark Questions
Q1. What was Lahore Resolution? [4]
Ans: The Lahore Resolution was passed on 23rd March 1940 during the All India Muslim League session at 
Minto Park, Lahore, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah. It demanded independent states for Muslims in the north￾western and eastern parts of India where they were in majority. The resolution gave a clear goal of a separate 
homeland, later known as Pakistan Resolution. It united Muslims under one demand and gave new direction to 
their struggle. This became the foundation of Pakistan’s creation in 1947.
Q2. What was August Offer? [4]
Ans: The August Offer was announced by the British Government on 8th August 1940 to gain Indian support in 
World War II. It promised Indians more political representation and a Constituent Assembly after the war to 
frame India’s constitution. However, it still kept all real power with the British Governor-General. The 
Congress rejected it demanding complete independence, while the Muslim League did not accept it without 
Muslim safeguards. The offer failed but showed Britain’s growing need for Indian cooperation.
Q3. What was Atlantic Charter? [4]
Ans: The Atlantic Charter was signed in August 1941 between U.S. President Roosevelt and British Prime 
Minister Churchill. It promised that after World War II, all nations would have the right to self-determination 
and freedom. Indian leaders hoped these principles would apply to India too. However, the British later said it 
was meant only for European nations, disappointing Indians. This led to greater resentment and increased 
demands for India’s independence.
Q4. What was Cripps Mission Plan? [4]
Ans: The Cripps Mission came to India in March 1942 under Sir Stafford Cripps, sent by Britain to get Indian 
support in World War II. It offered Dominion Status after the war and allowed provinces to separate from India 
if they wished. However, the Congress rejected it because it allowed partition, and the Muslim League rejected 
it because it didn’t guarantee Pakistan. The failure of this mission increased political tension. It also led 
Congress to start the Quit India Movement.
Q5. What was Quit India Resolution? [4]
Ans: The Quit India Resolution was passed by the Congress in August 1942 in Bombay, led by Mahatma 
Gandhi. It demanded that the British must leave India immediately and declared a mass civil disobedience 
movement. The British responded by arresting all major Congress leaders and using force to stop protests. The 
movement failed quickly but caused much unrest across India. It also allowed the Muslim League to strengthen 
its political position while Congress was suppressed.
Q6. What was Gandhi Jinnah Talk? [4]
Ans: The Gandhi–Jinnah Talks took place in September 1944 at Jinnah’s residence in Bombay to find a 
political solution for India’s future. Mahatma Gandhi represented the Congress, and Jinnah represented the 
Muslim League. Jinnah firmly stood by the Two-Nation Theory and demanded Pakistan, while Gandhi refused 
to accept India’s division. The talks ended without any agreement. However, it made Jinnah’s position as the 
sole spokesman of Muslims much stronger.

Q7. What was Simla Conference? [4]
Ans: The Simla Conference was held in June–July 1945 under the British Viceroy Lord Wavell at Simla. The 
aim was to form a new Executive Council in India with equal representation for Hindus and Muslims. The 
Muslim League demanded that only it should nominate all Muslim members, but Congress disagreed. Due to 
this disagreement, the conference failed. Its failure made it clear that cooperation between Congress and 
Muslim League was no longer possible.
Q8. What was Cabinet Mission Plan? [4]
Ans: Three members of cabinet (A.V Alexander, Lord Pathic Lawrence and Staford Cripps) were sent by the 
British Government in March 1946 to discuss India’s future and transfer of power. It proposed a united India 
with three groups of provinces having their own governments but under one central government for defense and 
foreign affairs. The Congress wanted a strong center, while the Muslim League wanted full independence for 
Muslim areas. Due to these differences, the plan failed. Its failure convinced Muslims that partition was the only 
solution.
Q9. What was Direct Action Day? [4]
Ans: The Direct-Action Day was announced by the Muslim League on 16th August 1946 to show their demand 
for a separate homeland (Pakistan). It was declared after the failure of the Cabinet Mission Plan, when the 
British and Congress rejected Muslim demands. Huge rallies and protests were held across India to show 
Muslim unity. Unfortunately, violence broke out in Calcutta, causing many deaths. This event made it clear that 
Hindus and Muslims could not live together peacefully.
Q10. What was 3rd June Plan? [4]
Ans: The 3rd June Plan was announced by Lord Mountbatten, the last British Viceroy, on 3rd June 1947. It 
clearly accepted the partition of India into two independent states, India and Pakistan. Provinces like Punjab and 
Bengal were to be divided based on religious majority, and referendums were held in NWFP to decide their 
future. Both the Congress and Muslim League accepted the plan. This plan finally led to the creation of Pakistan 
on 14th August 1947
Q11. What was Independence Act? [4]
Ans: The Indian Independence Act was passed by the British Parliament on 18th July 1947. It ended British rule 
in India and created two independent dominions, Pakistan and India, from 15th August 1947. Each dominion 
was given the right to make its own laws and constitution. The Act also ended the control of the British Crown 
over India. This act officially marked the birth of Pakistan, fulfilling the dream of millions of Muslims.
Q12. Who was Lord Mountbatten? [4]
Ans: Lord Louis Mountbatten was the last British Viceroy of India, appointed in March 1947 to arrange the 
transfer of power. He played a key role in preparing the 3rd June Plan, which led to the partition of India into 
India and Pakistan. Mountbatten worked closely with both Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah and 
Jawaharlal Nehru to ensure a peaceful handover. However, his plan was rushed, which caused violence and 
migration problems during partition. Despite this, he is remembered for supervising the birth of Pakistan on 
14th August 1947.

Q13. Who was Cyril Redcliff? [4]
Ans: Sir Cyril Radcliffe was a British lawyer who was sent to India in June 1947 to draw the boundary line 
between India and Pakistan. He had no prior knowledge of Indian geography or culture, yet he had to complete 
his work within five weeks. He led the Boundary Commission, dividing Punjab and Bengal based on religious 
majorities. His decisions left many people unhappy and caused mass migration and violence. The Radcliffe 
Line became the official border between India and Pakistan.

Q4. Why did Indian National Congress start the Quit India Movement? [7]

Q6. Why did Gandhi Jinnah Talk fail? [7]

Another reason for the failure was that Gandhi claimed to represent all Indians, including Muslims. Jinnah 
strongly disagreed, saying that the Congress only spoke for Hindus and not for Muslims. He argued that the 
Muslim League was the only true representative of the Muslims of India. Gandhi’s refusal to accept this 
angered Jinnah and created more distance between them. Hence, the talks failed because Gandhi did not accept 
the League’s political authority over Muslims.

two separate nations with different cultures and religions, and could not live under one government. Gandhi

disagreement between them. Therefore, the Gandhi–Jinnah Talks failed as Gandhi refused to accept the Muslim 
demand for a separate homeland.

CHATPER 12: EARLY MINISTRIES (1948 – 1969)
4 Mark Questions
Q1. Who was Liaquat Ali Khan? [4]
Nawabzada Liaquat Ali Khan was born in 1895 in Karnal (India) in a noble family and received his education 
from Aligarh University and later from Oxford University in England. After returning, he started his political 
career in the Indian Legislative Assembly and later joined the All India Muslim League, where he worked for 
the rights of Muslims. After independence, he became the first Prime Minister of Pakistan and played an 
important role in setting up Pakistan’s government and economy. In 1951, he was assassinated while delivering 
a speech in Rawalpindi.
Q2. Who was Khuwaja Nazimuddin? [4]
He was born in 1894 in Dhaka (now Bangladesh) and got his education from Aligarh University and Cambridge 
University in England. He started his career in politics with the Bengal Legislative Council and later joined the 
All India Muslim League, where he supported the Pakistan Movement. After Quaid-e-Azam’s death, he became 
Governor-General and later replaced Liaquat Ali Khan as Prime Minister. He passed away in 1964 in Dhaka.
Q3. Who was Malik Ghulam Mohammad? [4]
He was born in 1895 in Lahore and studied at Aligarh University, later becoming a successful accountant. He 
started his career in the Indian Finance Department and after independence, he became Pakistan’s first Finance 
Minister, helping to improve the economy. In 1951, after the death of Liaquat Ali Khan, he was made 
Governor-General and played an important role in politics. He died in 1956 in Karachi.
Q4. Who was General Iskander Mirza? [4]
He was born in 1899 in Bengal and after his early education he joined Sandhurst Military Academy in England. 
He began his career in the British Indian Army and later served in important administrative posts. After 
independence, he became the Governor-General and in 1956 was elected as Pakistan’s first President. He was 
removed from power in 1958 and died in 1969 in London.
Q5. Who was Field Martial General Ayyub Khan? [4]
He was born in 1907 in Haripur (Hazara) and received his military training from the Royal Military Academy 
Sandhurst in England. He started his career in the British Indian Army and after independence became the 
Commander-in-Chief of the Pakistan Army. In 1958, he took control of the government through martial law and 
introduced many reforms. He resigned in 1969 and died in 1974 in Islamabad.
Q6. What was Objective Resolution? [4]
The Objective Resolution was presented in 1949 by Liaquat Ali Khan to set guiding principles for Pakistan’s 
constitution. It declared that sovereignty belongs to Allah, and authority would be exercised by elected 
representatives. The resolution promised democracy, freedom, equality, and justice according to Islam. It also 
guaranteed religious freedom and rights for minorities. Some minorities opposed it, fearing religious 
dominance. Later, it became part of all constitutions of Pakistan, shaping its Islamic identity.

Q7. What was Basic Principle Committee? [4]
The Basic Principles Committee was formed in 1949 to help draft Pakistan’s constitution. It was responsible for 
suggesting the political and administrative structure of the country. The committee proposed a federal system 
with a strong center and equal representation. Its reports faced criticism, especially from East Pakistan. Due to 
opposition, several reports were revised. Its work later helped in forming the 1956 Constitution.
Q8. What was PRODA? [4]
PRODA stands for Public and Representative Offices Disqualification Act, introduced in 1949. It aimed to stop 
corruption among politicians and government officials. The law allowed the government to remove corrupt 
public representatives. However, it was often used for political victimization. Many politicians were 
disqualified without fair trials. As a result, it damaged democracy and increased political instability.
Q9. What was Minority Pact / Liaquat Nehru Pact? [4]
The Minority Pact was an agreement between Liaquat Ali Khan and Jawaharlal Nehru in 1950. It was made to 
protect minorities in both India and Pakistan after Partition violence. Both countries promised equal rights, 
safety, and religious freedom. It aimed to stop migration and restore trust between communities. The pact 
reduced violence for some time. However, long-term peace between the two states was not achieved.
Q10. What was One Unit Scheme? [4]
The One Unit Scheme was introduced in 1955 to merge all provinces of West Pakistan into one unit. Its main 
aim was to create equality between East and West Pakistan. It reduced the political power of smaller provinces.
Many people opposed it due to loss of provincial identity. The scheme increased political unrest in West 
Pakistan. It was finally abolished in 1970.
Q11. What was the Constitution of Pakistan 1956? [4]
The Constitution of 1956 was Pakistan’s first constitution, enforced on 23 March 1956. It declared Pakistan an 
Islamic Republic with a parliamentary system. The Prime Minister became the head of government. It provided 
fundamental rights and a federal structure. Political instability weakened its implementation. The constitution 
was abrogated in 1958 after the military coup.
Q12. What was the Constitution of Pakistan 1962? [4]
The Constitution of 1962 was introduced by General Ayub Khan after ending the 1956 Constitution. It was 
based on a presidential system with strong powers given to the President. The Prime Minister’s post was 
removed, and the President became head of state and government. The system of Basic Democracies was used 
for elections. It aimed to bring stability and strong leadership. However, it reduced public participation and 
increased dictatorship.
Q13. What was Green Revolution? [4]
The Green Revolution began in the 1960s to increase agricultural production in Pakistan. It introduced high￾yield seeds, fertilizers, modern machinery, and tube wells. The government supported farmers through loans 
and improved irrigation. Wheat and rice production increased rapidly. However, benefits mostly went to big 
landowners. This increased economic inequality between rich and poor farmers.

Q14. What was Basic Democracies System? [4]
The Basic Democracies system was introduced by Ayub Khan in 1959. It created a local government system 
with elected representatives called Basic Democrats. These representatives elected the President and members 
of assemblies. The system aimed to involve people at the grassroots level. In reality, it strengthened Ayub 
Khan’s control over politics. It reduced true democracy and public political freedom.
Q15. What was Tashkent Declaration? [4]
The Tashkent Declaration was signed in January 1966 after the 1965 Indo-Pak War. It was signed by President 
Ayub Khan of Pakistan and Prime Minister Lal Bahadur Shastri of India, with Soviet Union mediation. Both 
countries agreed to withdraw their armies to pre-war positions. They also promised to restore diplomatic 
relations and avoid future conflicts. The agreement aimed to bring peace and stability to the region. However, 
many Pakistanis were disappointed, believing Pakistan gained little from it.

7 Mark Questions
Q1. Why Objective resolution received a lot of criticism in Pakistan? [7]
Many regional politicians criticized the Objective Resolution because they felt it gave more power to the central 
government. Leaders from smaller provinces were afraid that their cultural and political rights would be 
ignored. They believed the Resolution did not clearly protect provincial autonomy, and this could lead to unfair 
treatment of their regions.
Religious scholars also raised concerns but from a different perspective. Some of them believed that the 
Resolution was not strong enough in making Pakistan an Islamic state. They thought it used vague words about 
Islam and did not fully explain how Islamic laws would be applied. This made them doubtful about whether the 
Resolution would really make Pakistan a truly Islamic country.
From East Pakistan’s perspective, the Resolution was also criticized because it did not reflect their majority 
status. The people of East Pakistan felt that their language and culture were being neglected. They believed the 
Resolution mainly focused on West Pakistan’s interests, which created feelings of inequality and division 
between the two wings of the country.
Q2. Why was Pakistan unable to frame its own constitution in the early years after independence? [7]
After independence, Pakistan faced serious political instability which delayed constitution-making. Muhammad 
Ali Jinnah died in 1948, and Liaquat Ali Khan was assassinated in 1951. These sudden losses created a 
leadership vacuum at the top. Frequent changes of prime ministers weakened continuity in decision-making. 
Political parties were inexperienced and often divided over key issues. As a result, no stable leadership existed 
to finalize a permanent constitution.
There were deep disagreements among leaders about the nature of the state and distribution of power. East and 
West Pakistan argued over representation and population-based voting. Religious and secular groups also 
disagreed on the role of Islam in the constitution. Provinces demanded more autonomy, while the center wanted 
strong control. These disagreements delayed consensus for many years. Hence, framing a constitution became a 
slow and difficult process.
In the early years, Pakistan faced serious administrative problems due to Partition. Millions of refugees had to 
be settled, and law and order had to be maintained. The government focused more on survival issues than 
constitution making. There was also a shortage of experienced civil servants and legal experts. Economic 
weakness further slowed institutional development. These emergency challenges delayed the framing of a 
permanent constitution.
Q3. Why there were so many governments between 1951 and 1958? [7]
After the assassination of Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan in 1951, Pakistan lost a strong and unifying leader. 
The leaders who came after him were not as powerful or popular. This created instability, as political leaders 
often struggled to gain the trust of the people and to control the government effectively. Because of this, 
governments kept changing frequently.
Another major reason was the rivalry between politicians and the Governor Generals. Leaders like Ghulam 
Muhammad and Iskander Mirza misused their powers by dismissing prime ministers whenever they disagreed 
with them. Instead of allowing democracy to work smoothly, they interfered in politics, which caused 
governments to fall again and again.

Lastly, there was no proper Constitution until 1956, which made the political system weak. Without clear rules, 
it was easy for those in power to remove governments and replace them. This lack of a strong constitutional 
system and political unity led to frequent changes in government between 1951 and 1958.
Q4. Why Ayyub Khan came in power in 1958? [7]
Ayub Khan came to power in 1958 because Pakistan’s political system had become very weak. There were 
frequent changes of prime ministers, and no government was able to work for long. This constant instability 
created an environment where people began to look for a strong leader who could bring order and stability.
Another reason was that Iskander Mirza, the President at that time, wanted to strengthen his own rule. He 
dismissed the assemblies and imposed Martial Law with the help of Ayub Khan. But soon, Ayub Khan proved 
stronger and more popular than him. As a result, Ayub Khan removed Iskander Mirza and took full control of 
the government.
Finally, Ayub Khan came to power because the army was the most organized and powerful institution in the 
country. The politicians were divided and weak, while the army had discipline and resources. Many people also 
believed that only the army could save Pakistan from political chaos. That is why Ayub Khan successfully 
established himself as the ruler in 1958.
Q5. Why Ayyub Khan shifted the capital from Karachi to Islamabad? [7]
Ayub Khan shifted the capital from Karachi to Islamabad because Karachi was located in the extreme south of 
Pakistan. It was very far from many other parts of the country, especially the northern areas. Islamabad was 
chosen as it is in the center of the country, which made it easier to connect and govern all regions.
Another reason was security. Karachi was a coastal city and was considered unsafe during war or foreign attack 
because it could easily be targeted from the sea. Islamabad, on the other hand, is surrounded by mountains and 
located inland, which made it a safer and more secure place for the capital.
Lastly, Karachi was already Pakistan’s biggest trade and business city. Keeping both trade and government in 
the same city was causing overcrowding and administrative problems. By shifting the capital to Islamabad, 
Ayub Khan wanted to separate the government from commercial activities and allow Karachi to grow as the 
main economic hub.
Q6. Why did Ayyub Khan fall from office? [7]
Ayub Khan fell from office because his political system, called “Basic Democracies,” was not truly democratic. 
People felt that they had no real voice in choosing their leaders, and opposition parties strongly criticized his 
rule. This lack of democracy reduced his popularity over time.
Another reason was the economic situation. In the beginning, his policies brought growth, but later the benefits 
went mostly to rich people and big industrialists. Poor people felt ignored, and the gap between rich and poor 
widened. This caused unrest among the public, especially students and workers.
Finally, the 1965 war with India also weakened Ayub Khan’s position. Although the government claimed 
success, many Pakistanis felt disappointed with the outcome of the Tashkent Agreement. Opposition leaders, 
especially Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, used this to turn people against Ayub Khan. Facing protests, strikes, and 
pressure from all sides, Ayub Khan resigned in 1969.
