CHATPER 13: CREATION OF BANGLADESH (1969 - 1971)
4 Mark Questions
Q. Who was Sheikh Mujeeb-ur-Rahman? [4]
Sheikh Mujeeb ur Rahman, known as the founder of Bangladesh, was born in 1920 at Tungipara in Gopalganj, Bengal. He 
got his early education from local schools, then studied at Islamia College Calcutta and Dhaka University, where he 
entered student politics. He joined the Awami League and became the main leader of East Pakistan, raising the Six Points 
in 1966 to demand autonomy for Bengalis. His party won the 1970 elections but was not given power, which led to the 
independence of Bangladesh in 1971 where he became Prime Minister and later President. In 1975, he was assassinated 
along with most of his family in Dhaka.
Q. Who was General Yahya Khan? [4]
General Agha Muhammad Yahya Khan was born in 1917 in Chakwal, Punjab. He received his early education from local 
schools and later joined the Indian Military Academy at Dehradun, becoming an officer in the British Indian Army. After 
independence in 1947, he served in the Pakistan Army and rose to the rank of Commander-in-Chief. In 1969, after Ayub 
Khan’s resignation, he became the President of Pakistan and ruled during the 1971 war, which resulted in the separation 
of East Pakistan and the creation of Bangladesh. He left power in 1971 and died in 1980 in Rawalpindi.
Q. What was Awami Muslim league? [4]
The Awami Muslim League was a political party formed in 1949 in Dhaka. Its founding leaders were Maulana Abdul 
Hamid Bhashani, Hussain Shaheed Suhrawardy, and Sheikh Mujeeb ur Rahman, who wanted to protect the rights of 
Bengalis. The party aimed to fight for social justice, economic equality, and provincial autonomy for East Pakistan. It 
became very popular after the Language Movement and the Six Points in 1966, demanding more powers for East 
Pakistan. In the 1970 elections it won a majority, but being denied power led to the independence of Bangladesh in 1971.
Q. What were Sheikh Mujeeb’s six points agenda? [4]
Mujeeb’s Six Points were presented in 1966 as a program to give East Pakistan more autonomy because Bengalis felt 
ignored by West Pakistan. The six demands included control over trade, foreign exchange, taxation, and separate accounts 
for East Pakistan, along with the right to make its own economic and trade policies. Moreover, he also demanded for the 
separate troops for East Pakistan. Leaders of West Pakistan strongly opposed these points, saying they would break the 
unity of the country. However, these Points became very popular in East Pakistan and gave Mujeeb massive public 
support. In the 1970 elections his party won a majority, but refusal to give him power led to the separation of East 
Pakistan and the creation of Bangladesh.
Q. What was Mukti Bahini? [4]
The Mukti Bahini was a guerrilla force formed in 1971 in East Pakistan during the independence movement of 
Bangladesh. It was organized by Bengali leaders and military officers who wanted to free East Pakistan from West 
Pakistan’s control. Its aim was to fight against the Pakistan Army and achieve independence for Bengalis. The Mukti 
Bahini carried out guerrilla attacks, destroyed communication lines, and worked with Indian forces during the 1971 war. 
Their struggle led to the victory of Bengali nationalists and the creation of Bangladesh in December 1971.

Q. What was Agartala Conspiracy Case? [4]
The Agartala Conspiracy Case was announced in 1968 by the government of Ayub Khan, accusing Sheikh Mujeeb ur 
Rahman and 34 others of planning with India in the city of Agartala to break East Pakistan. The people involved included 
civil servants, army officers, and Awami League members, with Mujeeb as the main accused. The main aim of the case 
was said to be the separation of East Pakistan and creation of an independent Bangladesh. The trial created anger in East 
Pakistan and huge protests began for Mujeeb’s release. In 1969 the case was withdrawn, Mujeeb was freed, and he 
became the most popular leader of East Pakistan.
7 Mark Questions
Q. Why East Pakistan wished to became independent from West Pakistan? [7]
One of the main causes of discontent was the language controversy. In 1948, the government declared Urdu as 
the only national language, completely ignoring Bengali, which was spoken by more than half of Pakistan’s 
population. This decision hurt the cultural pride and identity of the Bengali people, as they felt their language 
was being deliberately undermined. The sense of neglect pushed them to believe that only separation from West 
Pakistan would safeguard their language and culture.
Another important reason was the economic exploitation of East Pakistan. Although East Pakistan earned a 
large portion of foreign exchange through exports of jute, tea, and other products, most of the revenue was spent 
on developing West Pakistan’s industries and cities. Meanwhile, East Pakistan remained poor, with little 
investment in infrastructure, education, or jobs. This economic injustice led Bengalis to think that independence 
from West Pakistan was the only way to control their own resources.
East Pakistan also faced political discrimination despite having the majority population. Governments were 
mostly controlled by West Pakistanis, especially in the army, civil services, and central leadership. Even when 
East Pakistan won the majority of seats in elections, their leaders were not allowed to govern effectively. This 
constant denial of political power convinced Bengalis that they could only protect their democratic rights by 
separating from West Pakistan.
Q. Why the victory of Awami League in the elections of 1977 created a constitutional crisis in Pakistan? 
[7]
The victory of the Awami League in the 1970 elections created a constitutional crisis because it won a clear 
majority but was based only in East Pakistan. The party secured 160 out of 162 seats from East Pakistan but 
none from the West, showing a deep political and regional divide. This made it difficult to form a balanced 
national government. West Pakistani leaders feared total control by East Pakistan. Therefore, the election results 
created a constitutional crisis as both regions could not agree on forming one government.
Another reason for the constitutional crisis was that the Awami League’s Six Points Plan demanded almost full 
autonomy for East Pakistan. These points aimed to limit the federal government’s power over trade, currency, 
and defense. West Pakistani leaders, especially Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, believed this would break Pakistan into two 
parts. The disagreement over accepting the Six Points delayed constitution-making. Hence, the Awami 
League’s demands led to a serious constitutional deadlock between East and West Pakistan.
The crisis also arose because neither side was ready to compromise after the election. Sheikh Mujibur Rahman 
insisted on forming the government alone, while Bhutto refused to attend the National Assembly session unless 
power was shared. This political deadlock stopped the formation of a new constitution. The delay increased 
mistrust between the two wings of Pakistan. Therefore, the Awami League’s victory turned into a constitutional 
crisis as political cooperation completely broke down.

Q. Why did Sheikh Mujib ur Rahman become so popular in East Pakistan? [7]
Firstly, Sheikh Mujib became popular because he strongly spoke for the political rights of East Pakistan. He 
demanded democracy, fair elections, and equal participation of Bengalis in the government. People felt that 
West Pakistan was controlling politics and ignoring their voice. Mujib openly challenged this imbalance 
through speeches and movements. This made people see him as a fearless leader. Therefore, his struggle for 
political rights increased his popularity in East Pakistan.
Secondly, he gained support because he raised his voice against economic injustice faced by East Pakistan. He 
highlighted that most industries, jobs, and development funds were given to West Pakistan. Bengalis remained 
poor despite earning more foreign exchange through jute. Mujib promised economic autonomy so that East 
Pakistan could use its own resources. People trusted him to improve their living conditions. Hence, his stand on 
economic inequality made him very popular.
Thirdly, Sheikh Mujib became popular due to his Six Points agenda in which he demanded provincial autonomy 
and control over finances and trade for East Pakistan. The Six Points clearly addressed the daily problems of 
Bengalis in simple terms. Many people saw it as a peaceful solution to their long-standing issues. It united 
students, workers, and politicians under one demand. As a result, the Six Points greatly increased his popularity 
in East Pakistan.
Q. Why did the leadership of West Pakistan refuse to transfer power to Sheikh Mujibur Rahman after 
the 1970 elections? [7]
Firstly, West Pakistan’s rulers feared losing political control if power was transferred to Sheikh Mujib. The 
Awami League won a clear majority, but it was based in East Pakistan only. This meant the central government 
would be controlled by East Pakistan for the first time. West Pakistani leaders were not ready to accept this 
change. They believed their dominance would end. Therefore, fear of losing power stopped them from 
transferring authority to Mujib.
Secondly, West Pakistan opposed Sheikh Mujib because of his Six Point in which he demanded strong 
provincial autonomy for East Pakistan. West Pakistani leaders thought this would weaken the center and could 
break the country. They feared that Pakistan would become too loose to function properly. Military leaders also 
saw it as a threat to national unity. As a result, they refused to hand over power to Sheikh Mujib.
Thirdly, the military and political elite of West Pakistan did not trust Sheikh Mujib. They believed he was too 
close to Bengali nationalism rather than Pakistani unity. His strong support in East Pakistan worried them. They 
suspected he might eventually separate East Pakistan. This lack of trust created tension between both wings. 
Hence, mistrust of Sheikh Mujib was a major reason power was not transferred.

services. In the 1970 elections, Sheikh Mujib’s Awami League won the majority on the demand for autonomy through the

4 Mark Questions
Q1. Who was Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto? [4]
Ans: Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto was born on 5th January 1928 in Larkana, Sindh. He studied at the University of 
California, Berkeley, and later earned a law degree from Oxford University in England. Bhutto began his 
political career in the 1950s and became Foreign Minister under Ayub Khan, later founding the Pakistan 
People’s Party (PPP) in 1967. He served as President (1971–73) and then Prime Minister (1973–77) of Pakistan, 
introducing many reforms. In 1979, he was executed after a controversial trial under General Zia-ul-Haq’s 
military rule.
Q2. What was Simla Accord? [4]
Ans: The Simla Accord was signed on 2nd July 1972 between Pakistan’s Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto 
and India’s Prime Minister Indira Gandhi after the 1971 war. It aimed to restore peaceful relations and respect 
each other’s territorial integrity. Both countries agreed to solve all disputes, including Kashmir, through 
bilateral talks. Prisoners of war were to be released, and troops withdrawn from occupied areas. The accord 
helped normalize relations but failed to permanently resolve the Kashmir issue.
Q3. What was 1973 constitution? [4]
Ans: The Constitution of 1973 was passed under Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto and came into effect on 
14th August 1973. It made Pakistan a Federal Parliamentary Republic, with the Prime Minister as the chief 
executive and President as a ceremonial head. Islam was declared the state religion, and both Urdu and English 
were made official languages. It guaranteed fundamental rights and equality for all citizens. This constitution 
united the nation and is still the current constitution of Pakistan.
Q4. What is Pakistan People’s Party? [4]
Ans: The Pakistan People’s Party (PPP) was founded in 1967 by Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto in Lahore. Its slogan was 
“Roti, Kapra aur Makan” (Food, Clothing, and Shelter), showing its focus on the rights of the poor and working 
class. The party aimed to establish social justice, democracy, and equality in Pakistan. It played a major role in 
rebuilding the country after the 1971 war and introducing the 1973 Constitution. The PPP became one of 
Pakistan’s most influential political parties, later led by Benazir Bhutto after her father’s death.
Q5. What was security of tenure scheme? [4]
Ans: The Security of Tenure Scheme was introduced by Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto to protect government employees 
from unfair dismissal. Before this, many workers could lose their jobs due to political pressure or corruption. 
The scheme ensured that civil servants and employees could only be removed for valid reasons after proper
investigation. It aimed to create job security and encourage honest service. This reform improved confidence 
among public workers and made government jobs more stable.
Q6. What was Federal Security Force? [4]
Ans: The Federal Security Force (FSF) was created by Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto in 1972 to maintain law and order 
and provide security to government officials. It worked under the Interior Ministry and was meant to control 
political violence and unrest. However, later it was accused of being used for political purposes against 
opposition parties. The force became controversial due to alleged human rights abuses. It was finally disbanded 
by General Zia-ul-Haq after Bhutto’s removal from power.

Q7. Who was General Zia ul Haq? [4]
Ans: General Zia-ul-Haq was born in 1924 in Jalandhar, India, and he received his early education there before 
studying at St. Stephen’s College and joining military training. He served in the Pakistan Army after 1947 and 
rose through different posts until he became Chief of Army Staff in 1976. In 1977, he removed Prime Minister 
Bhutto and took control of the country, introducing martial law and later bringing Islamic laws and reforms into 
Pakistan. His rule continued for eleven years, during which he also supported the Afghan Mujahideen in the 
Soviet-Afghan War. He died in 1988 in a mysterious plane crash near Bahawalpur.
Q8. What was Operation Fair Play? [4]
Ans: Operation Fair Play was the military takeover led by General Zia-ul-Haq in 1977. It happened because the 
opposition parties claimed that the elections held by Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto were unfair and protests 
were spreading. The army stepped in, removed Bhutto from power, and imposed martial law across the country. 
General Zia said the operation was meant to restore peace and hold fresh, fair elections. The outcome was that 
Zia stayed in power for many years, and Pakistan came under long military rule.
Q9. What was Islamization? [4]
Ans: Islamization was a set of religious laws and reforms introduced by General Zia-ul-Haq during his rule in 
Pakistan. It began because Zia wanted to make the country’s legal and social system more in line with Islamic 
principles. New laws such as Zakat, Ushr, Hudood Ordinances, and Islamic banking were introduced. Schools 
and media were also encouraged to promote Islamic teachings. The outcome was that Pakistan’s society and 
laws became more strongly influenced by religion, and these changes continued even after Zia’s rule.
Q10. What was Ojhri Camp Incident? [4]
Ans: The Ojhri Camp Incident happened in 1988 when an ammunition storage camp in Rawalpindi, used during 
the Afghan-Soviet War, accidentally exploded. The camp was filled with weapons meant for the Afghan 
Mujahideen, and no proper safety measures were taken. When it blew up, rockets and shells flew into nearby 
areas of Islamabad and Rawalpindi, causing many deaths and injuries. The government faced strong criticism 
because people felt the camp was kept too close to the cities. The outcome was a big loss of life, damage to 
property, and greater pressure on the government for accountability.

7 Mark Questions
Q1. Why Bhutto adapted the policy of nationalization? [7]
Ans: Bhutto adopted the policy of nationalization because he wanted to reduce the gap between the rich and the 
poor. In Pakistan, most industries and businesses were owned by a few wealthy families, while the majority of 
people lived in poverty. Bhutto believed that by taking control of these industries, the government could use 
their profits for public welfare. This would create more equality in society. Therefore, he introduced 
nationalization to bring economic justice to the common people.
Another reason for nationalization was to strengthen government control over key industries and services. 
Bhutto wanted the state to manage important sectors like banks, schools, and factories to ensure fair prices and 
better planning. He believed private owners were exploiting resources for personal gain instead of national 
progress. By nationalizing major institutions, the government could direct them toward national development. 
Hence, this policy was meant to make the economy more stable and organized.
Bhutto also adopted nationalization to fulfill his socialist vision of “Islamic Socialism.” His political slogan was 
Roti, Kapra aur Makaan (food, clothing, and shelter) for every citizen. Nationalization, he believed, would help 
achieve these goals by providing basic needs through government programs. This policy also increased his 
popularity among the working class. Therefore, Bhutto introduced nationalization as part of his mission to 
create a more equal and welfare-based Pakistan.
Q2. Why Educational Reforms of Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto couldn’t achieve success? [7]
Ans: Bhutto’s educational reforms could not succeed because the government quickly nationalized all private 
schools and colleges. This sudden takeover created management problems, as the government did not have 
enough funds or trained staff to run these institutions properly. Many schools faced shortages of teachers and 
equipment. The quality of education began to fall instead of improving. Therefore, nationalization made the 
education system weaker instead of stronger.
Another reason for the failure was that education became overcrowded in urban areas especially after it was 
made free for everyone. The number of students increased rapidly, but there were not enough classrooms, 
teachers, or books to meet the demand. This led to poor learning environments and low-quality teaching. Many 
students could not get proper attention from teachers. Hence, the reforms failed because the government was not 
prepared for the large number of new students.
The educational reforms also failed because political influence and corruption entered the system. Many school 
appointments and promotions were made based on personal connections instead of merit. Discipline and 
motivation among teachers and students declined. As a result, the standard of education dropped across the 
country. Therefore, Bhutto’s educational reforms could not succeed as politics and poor management damaged 
the real purpose of improvement.

Q3. Why Industrial Reforms of Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto couldn’t achieve success? [7]
Ans: Bhutto’s industrial reforms could not succeed because the government took control of too many industries 
without proper planning. Many experienced owners and managers were removed, and government officers who 
replaced them did not have enough skills to run the factories. This caused a drop in production and poor-quality 
goods. Industries started making losses instead of profits. Therefore, nationalization damaged efficiency and led 
to the failure of the reforms.
Another reason for failure was that private businessmen lost trust in the government. After seeing many 
factories being nationalized, investors became afraid that their own businesses might also be taken away. 
Because of this fear, they stopped investing in new industries. This reduced job opportunities and slowed down 
economic growth in the country. Hence, the reforms failed because they discouraged private investment and 
hurt Pakistan’s industrial progress.
The industrial reforms also failed because political interference and corruption increased inside nationalized 
industries. Many appointments were made based on political connections instead of ability or experience. This 
led to mismanagement, wastage of money, and weak decision-making. Workers also became less motivated 
because they did not fear losing their jobs. Therefore, the reforms did not succeed as corruption and poor 
management destroyed the purpose of nationalization.
Q4. Why it was difficult for the Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto to be in power by the end of 1970s? [7]
Ans: It was difficult for Bhutto to stay in power by the late 1970s because many people were unhappy with his 
economic policies, especially nationalization. Factories and businesses were taken over by the government, 
which led to losses, unemployment, and slow economic growth. This caused frustration among workers, 
businessmen, and the middle class. People began to blame Bhutto for economic problems. Therefore, growing 
public dissatisfaction made his rule weak and unstable.
Another reason was that Bhutto faced strong opposition after the 1977 elections, which many parties claimed 
were rigged. The Pakistan National Alliance (PNA) started massive protests, marches, and strikes across the 
country. The situation became violent and out of control in many cities. The government struggled to maintain 
law and order. Hence, the political unrest made it very hard for Bhutto to continue in power.
It was also difficult for Bhutto to remain in power because he lost the support of the army, which was very 
important in Pakistan’s politics. Army officers were unhappy with Bhutto’s strict policies and his attempts to 
control them. When protests increased, the army felt that Bhutto could no longer manage the country. This led 
General Zia-ul-Haq to remove him through a military coup in July 1977. Therefore, the loss of army support 
made it impossible for Bhutto to stay in power.

Q5. How General Zia ul Haq came in power in 1977? [7]
Ans: General Zia-ul-Haq came to power in 1977 because Pakistan was facing serious political unrest after the 
general elections. Many opposition parties, united under the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA), accused Bhutto 
of rigging the elections. This led to large protests, strikes, and violence all over the country. The government 
failed to control the situation. Therefore, the army stepped in, giving Zia the excuse to take control to restore 
order.
Another reason was that Bhutto had lost the support of the army, which is very important for stability in 
Pakistan. Many senior officers were unhappy with his leadership style and policies. They believed Bhutto was 
becoming too powerful and difficult to work with. When the country fell into chaos, the army decided to act. 
Hence, Zia took advantage of this moment and removed Bhutto from power.
General Zia also came to power because he promised to act as a neutral leader and bring fresh elections. He 
claimed that military rule was only temporary and that he would fix the problems caused by political fighting. 
Many people were tired of the tension and welcomed this promise. This made it easier for Zia to take control 
without facing much resistance. Therefore, Zia-ul-Haq became the ruler by presenting himself as.
Q6. Why General Zia ul Haq introduced Islamization? [7]
Ans: General Zia-ul-Haq introduced Islamization because he wanted Pakistan’s laws and society to follow 
Islamic principles. He believed that since Pakistan was created in the name of Islam, its system should also be 
Islamic. Zia introduced Sharia courts, Islamic punishments, and promoted Islamic values in daily life. This 
helped him show that he was strengthening the country’s Islamic identity. Therefore, Islamization was 
introduced to make Pakistan’s system more Islamic.
Another reason for Islamization was that Zia wanted public support to strengthen his government. After taking 
power through a military coup, he needed a way to gain people’s trust and acceptance. By promoting Islam, he 
won the support of religious groups and many ordinary citizens. This helped him stay in power for a long time. 
Hence, Islamization also served as a political tool to gain popularity.
Zia also introduced Islamization because he wanted to unite the people of Pakistan under one religious’ identity. 
At that time, Pakistan faced political conflicts and social problems. Zia believed that Islam could bring unity, 
discipline, and stability to society. He encouraged Islamic education and practices to reduce divisions among 
people. Therefore, Islamization was used as a way to create national unity and strengthen the country.
Q7. Why was governing Pakistan becoming increasingly difficult for Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq towards the 
end of his rule? [7]
Ans: Firstly, there was a serious law and order situation, especially in Sindh. In cities like Karachi and 
Hyderabad, violence, sectarian riots, kidnappings for ransom, and drug trafficking increased. The arrival of 
Afghan refugees after the Soviet–Afghan War also made weapons and drugs such as heroin easily available. 
This rise in crime and violence made it harder for Zia to maintain stability in the country.
Secondly, a new political party, Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM), became popular among Urdu-speaking 
migrants from India living in urban Sindh. However, tensions grew between the Muhajir community and the 
Sindhi-speaking population. These tensions led to several violent clashes in Karachi and Hyderabad. Such 
ethnic conflicts weakened Zia’s control and made governance more difficult.

Thirdly, In April 1988, a huge explosion occurred at Ojhri Camp in Rawalpindi, killing many civilians. The 
Prime Minister, Muhammad Khan Junejo, announced a transparent investigation into the incident. Zia feared 
that the inquiry might blame senior military officers. To avoid losing military support, he dismissed Junejo’s 
government in May 1988. This action created a major political crisis and further weakened Zia’s authority.

Q1. Who was Benazir Bhutto? [4]
Ans: Benazir Bhutto was born in 1953 in Karachi, Pakistan, into a well-known political family as the daughter 
of Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, former Prime Minister of Pakistan. She studied at Harvard University in the USA and 
later at Oxford University in the UK, where she became active in student politics. After her father’s death, she 
entered politics and became the first woman Prime Minister of Pakistan in 1988. Her rule focused on 
democracy, women’s rights, and economic reforms, though she faced political challenges and corruption 
charges. Benazir Bhutto was sadly assassinated in 2007 during an election rally in Rawalpindi, ending a major 
chapter in Pakistan’s political history.
Q2. Who was Ghulam Ishaq Khan? [4]

began his career as a civil servant and became known for his honesty and administrative skill. He served as 
President of Pakistan from 1988 to 1993, taking office after General Zia-ul-Haq’s death. During his tenure, he 
oversaw political instability, frequent government changes, and economic challenges. Ghulam Ishaq Khan 
passed away in 2006 in Peshawar, remembered as a cautious and bureaucratic leader in Pakistan’s political 
history.
Q3. Who was Nawaz Sharif? [4]
Ans: Nawaz Sharif was born in 1949 in Lahore, Pakistan, into a successful industrial family involved in the 
steel business. He studied business and law at Government College and Punjab University in Lahore. Entering 
politics in the 1970s, he became Chief Minister of Punjab and later served as Prime Minister of Pakistan three 
times (1990–1993, 1997–1999, and 2013–2017). His rule focused on economic growth, infrastructure projects, 
and strengthening Pakistan’s nuclear program, though he faced corruption charges and political conflicts.
Q4. What was Train March? [4]

and show his popularity across Pakistan. After being removed from office as Prime Minister, Nawaz Sharif 
traveled from Karachi to Lahore by train, stopping at many stations to address large crowds. The march became 
a symbol of resistance against the government of Benazir Bhutto and demand for fair elections. Thousands of 
supporters joined him along the way, strengthening his political image and party unity. Therefore, the Train 
March helped Nawaz Sharif regain popularity and re-establish himself as a major national leader.
Q5. What was Kargil Conflict? [4]
Ans: The Kargil Conflict was a military clash between Pakistan and India that took place in 1999 in the Kargil 
region of Kashmir. Pakistani soldiers and Kashmiri fighters crossed the Line of Control (LoC) and occupied 
high mountain positions on the Indian side. This led to heavy fighting as India launched attacks to push them 
back. The conflict ended after international pressure, especially from the United States, made Pakistan withdraw 
its troops. Therefore, the Kargil Conflict increased tensions between the two countries and damaged trust even 
after years of peace talks.

Q5. Who was Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah? [4]
Ans: Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah was born in 1933 in Karachi, Pakistan, and served as the Chief Justice of 
Pakistan from 1994 to 1997. He joined the legal profession as a lawyer and later became a judge of the Sindh 
High Court and then the Supreme Court. During his tenure, he was known for his firm decisions and clashes 
with the government, especially with Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. His disagreements over judicial 
independence led to strong political and judicial conflicts. As a result, Sajjad Ali Shah was removed from office 
in 1997 after a controversial division within the Supreme Court itself.

7 Mark Questions
Q1. Why were there change in governments between 1988 and 1999? [7]
Ans: After General Zia died in 1988, the 8th Amendment gave the President strong power to remove elected 
leaders anytime. This meant even when people voted for a Prime Minister, the President or military could end 
their government if they were not happy. Benazir Bhutto and Nawaz Sharif both lost power this way, not 
because of elections, but by orders from above This link shows that government changes happened because real 
power stayed with unelected forces, not with the people's choice. So, democracy could not grow strong during 
these years.
Secondly, many elected leaders faced serious charges of corruption and failing to fix daily problems like jobs, 
prices, and electricity. When people saw no improvement in their lives, they lost trust and protested against the 
government. This public anger gave reasons for Presidents or courts to step in and dismiss the ruling party. 
Because leaders could not deliver good results, their governments fell before completing their term. This shows 
that poor performance and corruption directly caused frequent changes in power.
Thirdly, Political parties, especially PPP and PML-N, spent more time fighting each other than working for the 
country. Each side tried to weaken the other by complaining to the President, courts, or military. This constant 
rivalry created chaos and made it impossible for any government to finish its five-year term. As a result, 
governments kept changing not because of public votes, but because of behind-the-scenes power games. This 
link proves that lack of cooperation between leaders broke the democratic process.

Q1. To what extent was Benazir Bhutto successful in governing Pakistan between 1988 and 1990?

Explanation 2: Economic Challenges (Failure)
Explanation 3: Poor relations with President and Military (Failure)
Explanation 4: Pucca Qila Massacre (Failure)
Explanation 5: Challenges from the family (Failure)
Explanation 1 / Paragraph 1
After years of military rule, Benazir Bhutto’s government (1988–1990) restored democracy and civilian leadership in 
Pakistan. She encouraged freedom of speech and allowed political parties to work openly again. Her government also 
focused on social welfare and women’s rights, giving women more opportunities in jobs and politics. This created hope 
for a democratic future after General Zia’s dictatorship. Therefore, her greatest success was bringing back civilian rule 
and reviving public confidence in democracy.
Explanation 2 / Paragraph 2
Benazir Bhutto faced serious economic challenges, such as rising prices, unemployment, and corruption. Government 
departments were poorly managed, and foreign loans increased, putting pressure on the economy. Her promises of quick 
economic improvement could not be achieved due to weak administration. Many people became unhappy because living 
conditions did not improve. Therefore, her failure to control the economy weakened her government’s popularity 
and effectiveness.
Explanation 3 / Paragraph 3
Benazir Bhutto struggled to maintain good relations with President Ghulam Ishaq Khan and the military, who still held 
great power. Disagreements over government policies and appointments led to constant political tension. The military also 
felt her government was inexperienced and weak in decision-making. These conflicts limited her ability to govern freely 
and make independent choices. Therefore, her weak relationship with the army and president became a major 
reason for her government’s failure.
Explanation 4 / Paragraph 4
During Benazir’s rule, law and order worsened, especially in Karachi and Sindh, where political and ethnic violence 
increased. The government could not control crimes and clashes between political groups like the MQM and PPP, which 
led to tragic incidents such as the Pucca Qila massacre in Hyderabad (1988). This gave the opposition and military a 
reason to criticize her leadership. Ordinary people began to lose faith in her ability to maintain peace and stability. 
Therefore, the growing disorder in the country was a key failure that led to her government’s dismissal in 1990.
Explanation 5 / Paragraph 5
Benazir Bhutto also faced many personal and family challenges during her first term as Prime Minister. Her brother 
Murtaza Bhutto openly opposed her government from exile, accusing her of ignoring her father’s political vision. This 
created tensions within the Bhutto family and damaged the unity of the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP). The family disputes 
became public, which weakened her image as a strong leader. Therefore, internal family conflicts added extra 
pressure on Benazir and made it harder for her to focus on governing the country effectively.

Q2. To what extent was Nawaz Sharif successful in governing Pakistan between 1990 and 1993? Explain

During Nawaz Sharif’s first government (1990–1993), Pakistan saw some economic improvement through privatization 
and promotion of private businesses. He sold many state-owned industries to reduce government control and encouraged 
investment. Major development projects like the M2 Lahore–Islamabad Motorway and energy programs such as the Hub 
Power Project were launched. These efforts created jobs and improved Pakistan’s infrastructure, especially in transport 
and energy. Therefore, Nawaz Sharif was partly successful in boosting economic growth and promoting 
modernization in the country.
Explanation 2 / Paragraph 2
The Yellow Cab Scheme, launched by Nawaz Sharif in 1992, aimed to reduce unemployment by helping educated youth 
buy taxis through easy loans. It succeeded in giving many people self-employment and improving urban transport for a 
short time. However, the scheme later faced problems such as loan misuse, corruption, and poor loan recovery, which 
caused financial losses to banks. Many vehicles were sold illegally, and the program could not run effectively for long. 
Therefore, while the Yellow Cab Scheme showed good intentions to help the youth, weak management made it only 
a partial success for Nawaz Sharif’s government.
Explanation 3 / Paragraph 3
During Nawaz Sharif’s first government, Pakistan faced embarrassment due to the Bank of Credit and Commerce 
International (BCCI) scandal in 1991. The bank, which was partly owned by Pakistanis, collapsed after being accused of 
money laundering, corruption, and illegal financial dealings. Many Pakistani depositors and institutions lost huge amounts 
of money. The government was criticized for weak supervision and failure to protect Pakistan’s financial image. 
Therefore, the BCCI scandal became a major failure, showing poor control over financial affairs during Nawaz 
Sharif’s rule.
Explanation 4 / Paragraph 4
During this period, violence and political unrest increased, especially in Sindh and Karachi. The government could not 
control conflicts between ethnic and political groups, leading to the military’s involvement in law and order. People felt 
unsafe and blamed Nawaz Sharif for weak governance. The unrest damaged his credibility and created a negative image 
of his leadership. Therefore, his failure to ensure peace and stability led to disappointment and the end of his 
government in 1993.

Q4. To what extent was Nawaz Sharif successful in governing Pakistan between 1996 and 1999? Explain 
your answer. [14]
Marking Scheme:
Explanation 1: Nuclear Program (Success)
Explanation 2: 13th & 14th Amendments (Success)
Explanation 3: Clash with Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah / Supreme Court (Failure)

Explanation 1 / Paragraph 1
During Nawaz Sharif’s second government (1996–1999), his biggest success was conducting nuclear tests in May 1998 
after India’s tests. Despite international pressure and threat of sanctions, he decided to make Pakistan a nuclear power, 
ensuring national security and pride. The tests made Pakistan the first Islamic country with nuclear weapons, gaining huge 
public support. Although sanctions followed, people admired his courage and patriotism. Therefore, the nuclear tests 
were Nawaz Sharif’s most successful achievement, strengthening Pakistan’s defense and image worldwide.
Explanation 2 / Paragraph 2
Moreover, Nawaz Sharif passed the 13th and 14th Constitutional Amendments to strengthen his control over the 
government. The 13th Amendment removed the president’s power to dismiss an elected government under Article

However, Nawaz Sharif had a serious clash with Chief Justice Sajjad Ali Shah over the limits of government power. The

Therefore, Nawaz Sharif’s confrontation with the judiciary exposed his intolerance for criticism and became one of 
the key failures of his government.

Furthermore, the Kargil conflict in 1999 with India became a major failure. The army, led by General Pervez Musharraf,

later withdrew the forces after pressure from the United States, which angered the military leadership. Relations between 
him and General Musharraf completely broke down, and Nawaz’s later attempt to remove Musharraf while he was abroad
